Introduction

Compiling a project from source is the process of converting human-readable code into an executable file that your computer can run. This guide covers the common compilation workflow for C++ projects shared on Paste-co.de.

1. Prerequisites: Visual Studio

Almost all C++ based game security projects require Microsoft Visual Studio. While other IDEs exist, Visual Studio provides the most robust toolchain for Windows-based development.

Get the Community Edition (which is free) here: https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/

Important Note:When installing, make sure to select the "Desktop development with C++" workload in the installer, otherwise you will be missing the necessary compilers and libraries.

2. Opening & Configuring the Solution

After downloading the project source, look for a .sln (Solution) or .slnx file. Double-clicking this will open the entire project in Visual Studio.

  • Solution Configuration: Look at the top toolbar. By default, it might say "Debug". Change this to Release for optimal performance and smaller file size.
  • Solution Platform: Next to the configuration, ensure it is set to x64 (or x86 if the project is specifically 32-bit).
  • Build Command: Once configured, press the green "Play" button or go to Build - Build Solution.

Troubleshooting Common Errors

"MSB8020: The build tools... cannot be found"

This happens when the project was made with an older (or newer) version of Visual Studio. Right-click the Project in the Solution Explorer, select Retarget Projects, and select your current SDK version.

"Cannot open include file: '...': No such file or directory"

You are likely missing a library. Check if the project uses a package manager like Vcpkg or NuGet, or if it requires external SDKs like the DirectX SDK.

If you get errors relating to the logic of the source itself, fixing them often requires deep technical knowledge of the codebase.

Overview

Kernel-mode development represents the highest level of privilege on a Windows system. Developing and compiling drivers requires a specialized set of tools known as the Windows Driver Kit (WDK). Unlike standard user-mode applications, drivers have direct access to system memory and hardware, making them powerful but also critical to system stability.

In the context of game security research, "mapping" a driver refers to the process of loading an unsigned driver into memory. Windows requires all drivers to be digitally signed by a trusted authority to load through standard means. Mappers bypass this requirement by exploiting legitimate but vulnerable drivers.

map-driver:
Overview

KDMapper is an open-source tool that loads a Windows kernel driver into memory without registering it through the normal driver loading mechanism (SCM — Service Control Manager). This technique is known as manual mapping and is commonly studied in security research because it bypasses Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) without requiring test signing mode.

1. What Is Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE)?

Since Windows Vista 64-bit, Microsoft requires all kernel-mode drivers to be digitally signed with a certificate trusted by Microsoft. The kernel checks this signature before loading any driver via NtLoadDriver or the SCM. This prevents malicious code from running at ring-0.

DSE is enforced by CI.dll (Code Integrity) in the kernel. When a driver load is attempted, CI.dll verifies the PE authenticode signature. KDMapper bypasses this by never asking the kernel to load the driver through the normal path at all.

2. How KDMapper Works — The iqvw64e.sys Exploit

KDMapper exploits a vulnerability in a legitimate, Microsoft-signed Intel network driver: iqvw64e.sys. This driver exposes an IOCTL that allows user-mode code to perform arbitrary kernel memory reads and writes.

The process step-by-step:

  1. KDMapper drops iqvw64e.sys to disk and registers it as a service using the SCM.
  2. Since iqvw64e.sys is legitimately signed, Windows loads it normally.
  3. KDMapper sends IOCTLs to the vulnerable driver to allocate non-paged kernel memory (ExAllocatePool) for the target driver image.
  4. KDMapper manually maps the target driver's PE image into that allocation — resolving imports, applying relocations, just like a PE loader.
  5. Using the IOCTL's arbitrary write primitive, KDMapper calls the target driver's DriverEntry function pointer from kernel context.
  6. The legitimate iqvw64e.sys is then unloaded and deleted.
Why it works:The target driver never touches the DSE check path. It is placed directly into kernel memory and executed — the kernel's loader is never involved.

3. Building Your Driver for KDMapper

Your driver must be compiled for manual mapping — it cannot rely on the driver framework registering it. Key requirements:

  • No CRT (C Runtime): The CRT is not initialized. Avoid global constructors, memcpy from CRT, etc. Use kernel equivalents (RtlCopyMemory, RtlZeroMemory).
  • Disable stack cookies: Remove /GS (security cookies), as the cookie value won't be set up correctly without the CRT.
  • No RTTI or exceptions: Disable C++ exceptions (/EHsc off) and RTTI.
  • DriverEntry signature must match: NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT, PUNICODE_STRING)
// Minimal KDMapper-compatible DriverEntry #include <ntdef.h> #include <ntddk.h> NTSTATUS DriverEntry( PDRIVER_OBJECT DriverObject, PUNICODE_STRING RegistryPath ) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(DriverObject); UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(RegistryPath); // Your kernel code here return STATUS_SUCCESS; }

4. Running KDMapper

KDMapper is a command-line tool. Run from an elevated (Administrator) prompt:

kdmapper.exe C:\\path\\to\\your\\driver.sys

KDMapper will output the base address of your mapped driver if successful:

[+] iqvw64e loaded [+] Allocating memory for image (0x12000) [+] Image mapped at: 0xFFFF800012340000 [+] Calling DriverEntry: 0xFFFF800012341000 [+] iqvw64e unloaded
Detection Note:Modern kernel-level anti-cheat drivers monitor for the loading of iqvw64e.sysand flag it as suspicious. Microsoft has also added iqvw64e.sys to the Vulnerable Driver Blocklist in Windows Security.

5. Alternative: Test Signing Mode

For legitimate driver development without DSE exploits, enable test signing mode. This is the correct approach for development and testing:

# Run as Administrator — enables test signing bcdedit /set testsigning on # Load your test-signed driver sc create MyDriver type= kernel binPath= C:\\driver.sys sc start MyDriver

Test signing mode adds a watermark to the desktop and is obviously detectable by anti-cheat, but it is the proper method for driver development workflows.

updating-offsets:
Overview

Every time a game updates, its executable is recompiled. This means internal data structures shift around in memory — the offsets that pointed to a player's health or position at address 0x130 may now be at 0x148. This guide walks through the systematic process of locating new offsets after a patch.

This is the systematic process every developer follows to keep projects working after game updates.

1. Why Offsets Change

A game's player entity might be a C++ class like CPlayer. When the developers compile a new version, they may add, remove, or reorder class members. This shifts the byte position (offset) of every subsequent field.

For example, if the original struct was:

struct CPlayer { char name[64]; // offset 0x00 float health; // offset 0x40 float maxHealth; // offset 0x44 Vector3 position; // offset 0x48 int team; // offset 0x54 };

And the devs insert a new int flags field after name, every field below it shifts by 4 bytes. Your old health offset of 0x40 is now 0x44.

2. The Diffing Approach

The fastest method for experienced developers is binary diffing — comparing the old and new executable to see exactly what changed. Tools like Diaphora (IDA plugin), BinDiff, or even simple hex-diff tools can highlight which functions changed and by how much.

If a function that accessed your known offset only changed slightly (e.g., the offset operand in a mov rax, [rbx+0x130] instruction changed to 0x148), you can update your offset directly from the diff without needing to run the game at all.

Tip:Diaphora is free and integrates with both IDA Pro and Ghidra. Even if the full diff is noisy, filter to functions you know contain your offsets.

3. The Cheat Engine Method

For simpler offsets (health, ammo, coordinates), the live scan approach is faster:

  1. Attach Cheat Engine to the updated game process.
  2. First scan for the known value type — if health is a float and you have 100 HP, scan for Float: 100.0.
  3. Take damage in-game, then Next Scan for the new value (e.g., 75.0). Repeat until you have 1–3 addresses.
  4. Load that address into ReClass.NET and check the surrounding memory layout. Compare it to your old struct map — you'll quickly see if the layout shifted.
  5. Calculate the offset from the module base address - moduleBase = offset. Do a pointer scan if it's a dynamic address.

4. Using Pattern Scanning for Stability

Rather than hardcoding raw offsets, experienced developers use pattern scanning to locate offsets dynamically at runtime. A byte pattern (AOB — Array of Bytes) in the game's code section is more stable than a raw address because code rarely changes significantly between minor patches.

The workflow:

  1. In IDA/Ghidra, find the instruction that reads your offset (e.g., mov eax, [rcx+0x40]).
  2. Copy the surrounding bytes as a pattern, using ? for bytes that may vary (addresses, offsets themselves).
  3. In your tool, scan memory for this pattern at startup, then read the offset operand from the matched instruction.
// Pattern: 8B 81 ? ? ? ? (mov eax, [rcx+??]) // Read offset from bytes at pattern+2 uintptr_t patternAddr = PatternScan(moduleBase, moduleSize, "\x8B\x81\x00\x00\x00\x00", "xx????"); uint32_t healthOffset = *reinterpret_cast<uint32_t*>(patternAddr + 2);

5. Keeping an Offset Map

Maintain a version-controlled file (JSON, TOML, or a C++ header) that maps offset names to values, along with the game version they were verified on. This makes it trivial to diff your offset file between versions and see what shifted.

// offsets.hpp // Game version: 1.42.3 (2024-11-14) namespace Offsets { namespace CPlayer { constexpr uintptr_t health = 0x44; // float constexpr uintptr_t maxHealth = 0x48; // float constexpr uintptr_t position = 0x4C; // Vector3 (12 bytes) constexpr uintptr_t team = 0x58; // int constexpr uintptr_t isAlive = 0x5C; // bool } }

cheat-engine-beginners:
What Is Cheat Engine?

Cheat Engine (CE) is a multi-purpose tool originally written by Eric Heijnen ("Dark Byte"). At its core it is a memory scanner — it attaches to a running process and allows you to read, search, and write values anywhere in that process's virtual address space. Beyond scanning, it includes:

  • Debugger: A built-in x86/x64 debugger with breakpoints, step execution, and an assembler/disassembler (based on BeaEngine). You can pause a process mid-frame and inspect exactly which instruction wrote to an address.
  • Trainer Maker: Once you have stable addresses or pointer chains, CE lets you package them into a .CT (Cheat Table) file — a shareable XML document that encodes all your findings along with optional Lua scripts and hotkeys.
  • Structure Dissector: A tool for reverse-engineering in-memory C++ objects and structs by grouping contiguous addresses and watching which offsets change together.
  • Speed Hacks: CE can hook the Windows timer or the game's own timing functions to slow or accelerate execution — useful for frame-by-frame debugging.
Note:All techniques described here are for use on processes you own or have permission to analyze — such as single-player games you purchased, or purpose-built research environments. Studying memory structures is a core skill in game modding and security research.

First Scan: Finding a Value

The most common workflow begins with an Exact Value scan. Suppose your character has 250 HP displayed on screen. Open Cheat Engine, attach to the game process via the process selector, then:

  1. Set the Value Type to 4 Bytes (most game integers are 32-bit). If the value could be a float (e.g., 250.0f), choose Float.
  2. Set Scan Type to Exact Value.
  3. Type 250 in the value field and click First Scan. CE will read every committed memory page in the process and collect all addresses that currently hold the value 250.
  4. The results list may return thousands of hits — this is expected. Every variable that happens to equal 250 at this moment is included.

If you do not know the starting value — for example the health is shown as a bar but not a number — use the Unknown Initial Value scan type. CE takes a snapshot of all memory without filtering and records every address as a candidate. Subsequent scans then filter based on how values have changed relative to the snapshot.

Scan Type: Exact Value → knows the current number Scan Type: Unknown Initial → no idea what the number is Value Type: 4 Bytes → 32-bit signed integer (most common) Value Type: Float → 32-bit IEEE 754 float (e.g. 250.0) Value Type: 8 Bytes → 64-bit integer (modern engines) Value Type: 2 Bytes → 16-bit (older engines, inventory counts)

Narrowing Down Results

After the first scan you typically have far too many candidates. The trick is to change the game state — take some damage, heal, spend gold — and then run a Next Scan with a refined criterion. Repeat until only a handful of addresses remain.

  • Exact Value: You know the new precise value (e.g., after taking 30 damage, scan for 220). Eliminates everything that is not exactly 220 now.
  • Decreased Value: You know the value went down but not by how much (health dropped, money spent). Keeps addresses whose current value is lower than the snapshot.
  • Increased Value: The value went up (experience gained, item collected). Keeps addresses higher than snapshot.
  • Decreased By: You know the exact delta. Took 30 damage? Decreased By 30. Very precise — cuts results dramatically.
  • Increased By: Gained exactly 500 gold? Increased By 500.
  • Unchanged Value: Nothing happened between scans — keeps only addresses that have stayed the same. Use between action events to rule out noise.
  • Changed Value: Anything different from the snapshot — useful when you cannot control the change but know something changed.

A typical session: First Scan (exact 250) → take 30 damage → Next Scan (exact 220) → heal 50 → Next Scan (exact 270). After two or three iterations you should have 1–5 addresses remaining. The address that consistently follows your character's HP is your target.

Tip:Right-click any result and choose Browse this memory region to open the hex editor at that address. Nearby bytes often reveal adjacent fields in the same struct (e.g., mana right after HP).

The Address List and Freezing Values

Once you have found the correct address, double-click it (or press the red arrow button) to add it to the Address List at the bottom of the CE window. This list is your workspace — you can rename entries, change their value, and most importantly freeze them.

Freezing works by ticking the checkbox next to an entry. When frozen, CE's background thread repeatedly writes your chosen value back to that address at a high frequency (default ~30 writes/sec). The game's own code may still decrement HP, but CE immediately overwrites it — effectively making the value appear static.

Address List workflow: 1. Double-click result → appears in address list with current value 2. Double-click the "Value" column → type a new value → press Enter The game memory is immediately written with your new value. 3. Tick the checkbox → value is now FROZEN (CE rewrites it continuously) 4. Right-click entry → "Change record" → rename it (e.g. "Player HP") 5. Right-click entry → "Set/remove hotkey" → assign a key to toggle freeze

You can also set a freeze type: some entries should only ever increase (e.g., a resource you want to accumulate) or only decrease. Right-click and choose Change freeze type to control direction.

Pointer Scanning — Why Addresses Break and How Pointer Chains Solve It

The address you found with scanning is a dynamic heap address. Every time you restart the game, the memory allocator places game objects at different locations. Your saved address becomes invalid — you have to scan all over again.

The solution is a pointer chain. The game engine itself maintains stable, static pointers (usually in the .data segment of the EXE or a DLL) that eventually lead to the dynamic object you care about. A pointer chain looks like this:

Static base address (always the same, e.g. "game.exe"+0x12A4F0) → points to a Player Manager object at 0x1A3C0000 + offset 0x58 → points to local Player object at 0x1A3C8800 + offset 0x10C → the HP integer value In CE address list notation: [["game.exe"+0x12A4F0]+0x58]+0x10C

To find this chain, use CE's built-in Pointer Scanner:

  1. With your dynamic HP address in the address list, right-click it and choose Pointer scan for this address.
  2. Configure max level (depth of chain, typically 4–6) and max offset per level (usually 0x500 or 0x1000). Leave only static base addresses checked.
  3. Save the scan result (.ptr file). CE will enumerate thousands of candidate chains.
  4. Restart the game, reopen the .ptr file, and run Rescan pointer with the new dynamic address for HP. Any chain that still resolves correctly across restarts is valid.
  5. After two or three restarts, you will typically be left with one or a few valid chains. Add the shortest one (fewest offsets) to your address list — it is the most stable.
Note:You can also use CE's "Find out what writes to this address" debugger feature to locate the instruction that modifies HP. This instruction is in compiled game code at a stable offset from the module base — which gives you an even more reliable anchor point for reverse engineering the surrounding data structures.

Creating a Cheat Table (.CT File) and Sharing It

A Cheat Table (.CT) is a compressed XML file that stores your entire CE session: address list entries, pointer chains, Lua scripts, and hotkey bindings. It is the standard distribution format for CE-based mods.

To save a table: File → Save. To load one someone else made: File → Open then attach to the target process. CE will automatically resolve all pointer chains relative to the current session.

<!-- Simplified .CT XML structure (inside the compressed file) --> <CheatTable> <CheatEntries> <CheatEntry> <Description>Player HP</Description> <VariableType>4 Bytes</VariableType> <Address>"game.exe"+12A4F0</Address> <Offsets> <Offset>10C</Offset> <!-- last offset applied first --> <Offset>58</Offset> </Offsets> <CheatType>1</CheatType> <!-- 1 = frozen --> <CustomValue>9999</CustomValue> </CheatEntry> </CheatEntries> <LuaScript> -- Runs when the table activates print("Table loaded for MyGame v1.2") </LuaScript> </CheatTable>

CE's embedded Lua engine (Lua 5.3) lets you write activation scripts that auto-attach to processes, read addresses dynamically, create custom UI forms, and react to game events. Complex tables for modern games are essentially small Lua programs layered on top of CE's scanning infrastructure.

Community tables are shared on sites like FearLess Cheat Engine and the official CE forum. When studying a published table, examining the Lua scripts and pointer chains is an excellent way to understand how experienced researchers structure their findings — and how to extend them to newer game versions when offsets shift after an update.

Further Reading:Cheat Engine ships with a built-in tutorial process (Help → Cheat Engine Tutorial) that guides you through 8 progressively harder scanning challenges, including pointer levels and code injection. Working through all 8 steps is the fastest way to build foundational fluency.

dev-environment-setup:
1. Overview of the Tool Stack

Game security research requires a layered toolchain — each tool fills a specific role in the workflow. Understanding why each tool exists helps you choose the right one for a given task.

  • Visual Studio 2022 — The primary IDE and compiler for writing research tools in C++. MSVC is essential because it produces binaries that interoperate cleanly with Windows internals and the MSVC runtime that most commercial games use.
  • Cheat Engine — A memory scanner and debugger with a rich scripting environment (Lua). Indispensable for finding game values at runtime, building pointer maps, and rapid prototyping of memory offsets before committing them to C++.
  • x64dbg — An open-source, actively maintained user-mode debugger for 32-bit and 64-bit Windows binaries. More approachable than WinDbg for most game RE tasks, with an excellent plugin ecosystem (xAnalyzer, ScyllaHide, etc.).
  • IDA Pro / Ghidra — Static disassemblers and decompilers. IDA Pro is the industry standard (paid); Ghidra is the NSA-released open-source alternative with a capable decompiler. Both can import PDB files for symbol-assisted analysis.
  • ReClass.NET — A tool for reconstructing C++ class layouts from a live process. It lets you assign types and names to unknown memory regions, building a visual class diagram while the game runs.
Note:All tools listed here are legitimate software used by professional security researchers, reverse engineers, and game modding communities. Always research and comply with the terms of service of any software you study.

2. Installing Visual Studio 2022 with the Right Workloads

Download the Visual Studio 2022 Community installer from visualstudio.microsoft.com. When the workload selector opens, you need two specific workloads for game security research:

  • Desktop development with C++ — This includes the MSVC compiler (cl.exe), the linker (link.exe), the C++ Standard Library, and the Windows Runtime components. This is the non-negotiable core workload.
  • Windows 11 SDK (10.0.22621.0 or later) — Provides windows.h, WinAPI headers, and the platform toolset. Select the latest SDK available in the optional components panel on the right.

Optional but recommended: install the C++ Address Sanitizer component (listed under individual components) for catching memory corruption bugs in your own research tools.

After installation, verify the compiler is working:

# Open a Developer Command Prompt (search "Developer Command Prompt" in Start) cl.exe /? # You should see output like: # Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.38.xxxxx for x64

3. Setting Up a Test Virtual Machine

Running experimental code directly on your daily driver machine is a significant risk — kernel-mode code bugs can cause BSODs, and research tools can corrupt system state. A dedicated test VM isolates your work environment. Here are the three main options:

  • Windows Sandbox — Built into Windows 10/11 Pro and Enterprise. Launches a lightweight, isolated Windows environment that is destroyed on close. Ideal for quick tests, but has no persistence and limited graphics support (no DirectX 12), which makes it unsuitable for running actual games.
  • VirtualBox (Oracle) — Free, cross-platform hypervisor. Supports snapshots, which are essential for research — snapshot a clean state before running anything dangerous, and roll back instantly if something goes wrong. Enable "Nested VT-x/AMD-V" if you need to run hypervisor-aware code inside the VM.
  • Hyper-V — Microsoft's native Type-1 hypervisor, built into Windows Pro/Enterprise. Offers enhanced session mode for better graphics and clipboard sharing. Works well alongside WSL2. Checkpoint (snapshot) support is built in.

For most researchers, VirtualBox with snapshots is the best starting point. Recommended VM configuration for a research target:

  • 4–8 GB RAM assigned to the VM
  • 128 MB VRAM, enable 3D acceleration (required for DirectX)
  • Windows 10 22H2 or Windows 11 22H2 guest
  • Snapshot named clean-baseline immediately after OS install + tool setup, before any research begins
  • Shared folder mapped to a specific research/ directory on the host for easy file transfer
Warning:Never run kernel-mode drivers (e.g., a custom ring-0 driver you are writing) without first taking a VM snapshot. A bug in ring-0 code will crash the entire guest OS, and without a snapshot you will lose your work state.

4. Configuring Visual Studio for Research Projects

A default Visual Studio C++ project needs several adjustments before it is suitable for game security research work. The following settings apply to Project → Properties in the IDE, with the Release | x64 configuration selected.

General settings:

Configuration Properties > General Platform Toolset: Visual Studio 2022 (v143) Windows SDK Version: 10.0.22621.0 (or latest) Output Directory: $(SolutionDir)bin\$(Platform)\$(Configuration)\ Intermediate Directory: $(SolutionDir)obj\$(Platform)\$(Configuration)\

C/C++ → Code Generation:

Configuration Properties > C/C++ > Code Generation Runtime Library: Multi-threaded (/MT) -- Use /MT for Release. This statically links the CRT, removing the -- dependency on VCRUNTIME140.dll being present on the target machine. -- /MTd for Debug builds. Security Check: Disable Security Check (/GS-) -- /GS adds stack canaries. Disable only if you are studying stack -- layout precisely; leave enabled for production research tools. Enable Enhanced Instruction Set: Advanced Vector Extensions 2 (/arch:AVX2) -- Match this to the target machine's CPU capabilities.

Linker settings:

Only do this in controlled VM environments.

What Are Offsets and Why Do They Matter?

When a game runs, it allocates objects in memory — player entities, physics bodies, UI state, etc. These objects are C++ classes or structs laid out contiguously in RAM. An offset is the byte distance from the start of a structure to a particular member field. For example, if a PlayerEntity struct starts at address 0x12340000 and the health field is 0x100 bytes into the struct, then the absolute address of health is 0x12340100.

The problem is that the struct's base address changes every time the game restarts (ASLR — Address Space Layout Randomization). What stays stable across sessions are:

  • Module base offsets — the offset of a global variable from the start of the game's loaded module (.exe or .dll). The module base address varies, but the offset within it is fixed at compile time.
  • Pointer chains (multi-level pointers) — a static global pointer stored at a fixed module offset that points to a heap-allocated object, which in turn contains another pointer, and so on. Tools like Cheat Engine call these "pointer scans."
  • Member offsets within a struct — the byte distance from the struct's base to each field, which is determined at compile time and never changes between game builds of the same version.

Understanding this distinction — between absolute addresses (unstable) and relative offsets (stable) — is the foundation of any memory-based workflow.

Setting Up ReClass.NET

ReClass.NET is open source and maintained on GitHub under the ReClassNET/ReClass.NET repository. Download the latest release ZIP, extract it, and run ReClass.NET.exe as Administrator — elevated privileges are required to open handles to other processes with PROCESS_VM_READ access rights.

  1. Launch your target game and let it reach a gameplay state where the data you want to inspect is live in memory.
  2. In ReClass.NET, go to File → Open Process (or press Ctrl+O). A process list dialog appears. Select your game's process — typically the main .exe name.
  3. A new node view opens, starting at address 0x0000000000000000. This is a blank class that you will populate with memory reads once you have a target address.
  4. Optionally configure the "Settings" to show the module name alongside each address, which makes it easier to calculate stable module-relative offsets.
Note:Some anti-cheat protected games will terminate or flag the process if ReClass.NET attaches. Always conduct memory research in offline/single-player modes or on isolated research environments. Never attach to live competitive multiplayer sessions.

Scanning with Cheat Engine First

ReClass.NET is a structural inspector, not a scanner. You first need to know the address of something interesting before you can explore the surrounding memory layout. Cheat Engine excels at this initial discovery phase.

  1. Open Cheat Engine, attach it to the game process, and perform a scan for your target value — for example, current health as a 4-byte float. Take damage, scan for the new value. Repeat until you narrow down to one or a handful of addresses.
  2. Right-click a promising address in Cheat Engine and choose Find out what writes to this address. Apply damage again. The debugger window will show the instruction that wrote to the health field — this confirms you have the right address.
  3. Copy the address (e.g., 0x1FE3A2B4C0). Switch to ReClass.NET.
  4. In ReClass.NET, right-click the root class node and choose Change Address. Paste the address. ReClass will immediately begin reading 512 bytes of memory starting from that address and display them as a grid of nodes.

At this point you are looking at the raw bytes of whatever object lives at that address. The goal is to figure out whether you're looking at the field itself or the object that contains the field. If the address is your health float directly, you likely want to walk the memory backwards to find the object's base — subtract small amounts (try 0x10, 0x20, 0x40, etc.) and look for a vtable pointer (a pointer-sized value that points into the game's code section) at offset 0x00, which is the hallmark of a C++ polymorphic object.

Reading the Class / Struct Layout

Once you have the object base loaded in ReClass.NET, each row in the node grid represents one node (field). By default all nodes render as Hex 8 (8 bytes of raw hex). Your job is to right-click each node and assign it the correct type. Common types you will encounter:

  • Pointer (Ptr64 / Ptr32) — a value that is itself an address pointing elsewhere. If you see a value like 0x00007FF6AABBCCDD in a 64-bit process, it's almost certainly a pointer. You can "follow" it by right-clicking → Create Class at Pointer.
  • Float32 — health, speed, position components, timers. Values between roughly ±100,000 that change smoothly.
  • Int32 / UInt32 — ammo counts, enum states, flags bitmasks, item IDs.
  • Vector3 (Vec3) — three consecutive float32 values representing X, Y, Z. ReClass.NET has a built-in Vec3 node type. World-position fields are almost always Vec3 at a recognizable offset like 0x28, 0x38, or 0x78.
  • Bool / Byte — single-byte flags (is_dead, is_crouching, team_id).

Double-click a node to rename it. Build up your class definition field by field. As you rename and type nodes, ReClass.NET automatically shows the offset of each field in the leftmost column — this is the offset you will export to your code. For example, after analysis you might document:

// Reconstructed layout of PlayerEntity (0x500 bytes total) // Offset Size Name // 0x0000 8 vftable (pointer to vtable) // 0x0008 8 pEntityList (pointer) // 0x0028 12 vecOrigin (Vector3 - world position X,Y,Z) // 0x0034 12 vecVelocity (Vector3) // 0x0088 4 flHealth (float) // 0x008C 4 flMaxHealth (float) // 0x0090 4 iTeamNum (int32) // 0x0094 1 bAlive (bool) // 0x00A0 4 iAmmoCount (int32) // 0x00C0 8 pWeapon (pointer to WeaponEntity)

Exporting Offsets to C++ Code

Once you have documented your offsets, you express them in C++ as typed constants and use pointer arithmetic withReadProcessMemory (for external tools) or direct dereferencing (for internal DLLs). Below is a complete example of an external reader using the offsets discovered above.

#include <Windows.h> #include <cstdint> #include <cstdio> // ─── Offsets (discovered via ReClass.NET) ────────────────────────────────── namespace offsets { // From module base to the static pointer that holds the entity list root constexpr uintptr_t entityList = 0x01A2B3C0; // example — find via pointer scan // From a PlayerEntity base address to each member field constexpr uintptr_t vecOrigin = 0x0028; constexpr uintptr_t vecVelocity = 0x0034; constexpr uintptr_t flHealth = 0x0088; constexpr uintptr_t flMaxHealth = 0x008C; constexpr uintptr_t iTeamNum = 0x0090; constexpr uintptr_t bAlive = 0x0094; } // ─── Helpers ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── struct Vec3 { float x, y, z; }; // Read T bytes from a remote process at 'address' template <typename T> T RPM(HANDLE hProc, uintptr_t address) { T value{}; ReadProcessMemory(hProc, reinterpret_cast<LPCVOID>(address), &value, sizeof(T), nullptr); return value; } // Dereference a pointer chain: // base + offset[0] → ptr1 // ptr1 + offset[1] → ptr2 ... → final address uintptr_t ResolvePointerChain(HANDLE hProc, uintptr_t base, const std::initializer_list<uintptr_t>& offsets) { uintptr_t addr = base; for (auto off : offsets) { addr = RPM<uintptr_t>(hProc, addr) + off; } return addr; } // ─── Main ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── int main() { // Attach to game (see module base guide for GetModuleBaseAddress) HANDLE hProc = OpenProcess(PROCESS_VM_READ, FALSE, /* pid */ 12345); uintptr_t moduleBase = 0x7FF600000000; // obtained from TH32 snapshot // Resolve the local player entity pointer uintptr_t localPlayer = ResolvePointerChain(hProc, moduleBase, { offsets::entityList, 0x0, 0x58 }); // example multi-level chain if (!localPlayer) { puts("Failed to resolve local player pointer."); return 1; } // Read individual fields Vec3 origin = RPM<Vec3> (hProc, localPlayer + offsets::vecOrigin); float health = RPM<float>(hProc, localPlayer + offsets::flHealth); float maxHealth = RPM<float>(hProc, localPlayer + offsets::flMaxHealth); int team = RPM<int> (hProc, localPlayer + offsets::iTeamNum); bool alive = RPM<bool> (hProc, localPlayer + offsets::bAlive); printf("Position : (%.1f, %.1f, %.1f)
", origin.x, origin.y, origin.z); printf("Health : %.0f / %.0f
", health, maxHealth); printf("Team : %d | Alive: %s
", team, alive ? "yes" : "no"); CloseHandle(hProc); return 0; }

Pointer Scanning for Stable Multi-Level Pointers

A single absolute address for a heap-allocated object changes every session. To get a persistent path to your data, you need a pointer chain that starts at a statically addressed location (within the game module) and chains through heap pointers via known offsets. Cheat Engine's Pointer Scanner automates this discovery.

  1. With the target address still highlighted in Cheat Engine, go to Memory View → Tools → Pointer Scanner → Scan for pointers pointing to this address.
  2. Configure: Max level = 4–5, Max offset per level = 0x800 (increase for deeper chains). Check "Only find paths with static base" — this forces the first pointer in the chain to be within the loaded module image, giving you a stable starting point.
  3. Save the results. Restart the game. Re-scan the pointer list against the new address of the same value. Surviving results are stable pointer chains.
  4. A stable result looks like: game.exe+0x01A2B3C0 → +0x58 → +0x10 → +0x88. This means read a pointer at moduleBase + 0x01A2B3C0, add 0x58, follow that pointer, add 0x10, follow again, and the health float lives at the final address plus 0x88.

In ReClass.NET, you can visualize the same chain by following pointers level by level — each "Create Class at Pointer" operation drills one level deeper. Once the full chain is mapped, export the offset constants and encode them as an initializer list in the ResolvePointerChain function shown above.

Note:Offsets are version-specific. When a game updates, structures may be reordered or padded differently. Always re-verify offsets after patches by repeating the scan + ReClass inspection workflow. Automated offset scanners (pattern scanning for known byte sequences in the binary) can help re-find offsets quickly after updates.

External vs Internal: Architecture Overview

Memory-based game tools fall into two architectural categories, each with distinct tradeoffs:

  • Internal (injected DLL) — a .dll is injected into the game's process and runs inside its address space. Direct memory access is trivial (just dereference a pointer), function hooking is straightforward, and performance is high. However, DLL injection is highly visible: anti-cheat scans the module list and checks code integrity.
  • External (separate process) — runs as a completely independent .exe. It reads and writes the game's memory via Windows kernel cross-process APIs (ReadProcessMemory /WriteProcessMemory). No code runs inside the game process. The handle to the game process is the attack surface — anti-cheat monitors who holds open handles with PROCESS_VM_READ orPROCESS_VM_WRITE access.

External tools are conceptually simpler and easier to study. They require only standard Windows headers (Windows.h, TlHelp32.h) and no special kernel drivers. From a defense perspective, understanding them helps game security engineers decide what handle access patterns to monitor.

Getting a Process Handle with OpenProcess

Everything starts with obtaining a handle to the target process. The Windows API function OpenProcess takes a desired access mask, an inheritance flag, and a process ID (PID). You first need to find the PID by enumerating running processes.

#include <Windows.h> #include <TlHelp32.h> #include <cstdint> #include <string> #include <stdexcept> // Returns the PID of the first process matching processName (e.g., "game.exe") DWORD GetProcessId(const std::wstring& processName) { HANDLE hSnap = CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0); if (hSnap == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) throw std::runtime_error("CreateToolhelp32Snapshot failed"); PROCESSENTRY32W pe{}; pe.dwSize = sizeof(pe); if (Process32FirstW(hSnap, &pe)) { do { if (processName == pe.szExeFile) { CloseHandle(hSnap); return pe.th32ProcessID; } } while (Process32NextW(hSnap, &pe)); } CloseHandle(hSnap); return 0; // not found } // Open a handle with VM read/write access HANDLE OpenGameProcess(DWORD pid) { HANDLE hProc = OpenProcess( PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_VM_WRITE | PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION, FALSE, // don't inherit handle pid ); if (!hProc) throw std::runtime_error("OpenProcess failed — check privileges"); return hProc; } // Usage: // DWORD pid = GetProcessId(L"game.exe"); // HANDLE hProc = OpenGameProcess(pid);
Note:PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS is technically convenient but requests more rights than necessary and is more detectable. Prefer requesting only PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_VM_WRITE | PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION— the principle of least privilege applies in security research too.

Reading Memory with ReadProcessMemory

ReadProcessMemory copies bytes from another process's virtual address space into your own buffer. The function signature is:

BOOL ReadProcessMemory( HANDLE hProcess, // handle obtained from OpenProcess LPCVOID lpBaseAddress, // address in TARGET process to read from LPVOID lpBuffer, // your local buffer to receive the data SIZE_T nSize, // number of bytes to read SIZE_T* lpNumberOfBytesRead // actual bytes read (can be NULL) );

The ergonomic pattern is a templated wrapper so you can read any type cleanly:

// Generic typed read — returns T by value, zero-initialised on failure template <typename T> T Read(HANDLE hProc, uintptr_t address) { T value{}; ReadProcessMemory( hProc, reinterpret_cast<LPCVOID>(address), &value, sizeof(T), nullptr ); return value; } struct Vec3 { float x, y, z; }; // Reading concrete game values float health = Read<float> (hProc, playerBase + 0x0088); float maxHp = Read<float> (hProc, playerBase + 0x008C); Vec3 position = Read<Vec3> (hProc, playerBase + 0x0028); int teamNum = Read<int> (hProc, playerBase + 0x0090); bool isAlive = Read<bool> (hProc, playerBase + 0x0094); printf("Pos: (%.1f, %.1f, %.1f) HP: %.0f/%.0f Team: %d\n", position.x, position.y, position.z, health, maxHp, teamNum);

For bulk reads (e.g., reading an entire entity struct at once to reduce syscall overhead), read the whole struct into a local shadow copy and then access fields from it — this is both faster and more cache-coherent:

#pragma pack(push, 1) // match game's struct packing struct PlayerEntity { uint8_t _pad0[0x28]; Vec3 vecOrigin; // +0x28 Vec3 vecVelocity; // +0x34 uint8_t _pad1[0x50]; float flHealth; // +0x88 float flMaxHealth; // +0x8C int32_t iTeamNum; // +0x90 bool bAlive; // +0x94 }; #pragma pack(pop) PlayerEntity shadow = Read<PlayerEntity>(hProc, playerBase); // Now access shadow.flHealth, shadow.vecOrigin, etc. locally — zero RPM calls

Writing Memory with WriteProcessMemory

WriteProcessMemory is the write counterpart. It requires the target memory page to be writable (PAGE_READWRITE or PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE). Heap-allocated game data is almost always writable; code pages are not (and modifying them is a separate, more involved topic).

// Generic typed write template <typename T> bool Write(HANDLE hProc, uintptr_t address, const T& value) { SIZE_T written = 0; return WriteProcessMemory( hProc, reinterpret_cast<LPVOID>(address), &value, sizeof(T), &written ) && written == sizeof(T); } // Modifying game state fields float newHealth = 100.0f; bool ok = Write<float>(hProc, playerBase + 0x0088, newHealth); // Writing a Vec3 position (teleportation) Vec3 newPos = { 512.0f, 0.0f, 128.0f }; Write<Vec3>(hProc, playerBase + 0x0028, newPos); // Freeze health at max: write maxHealth value into health field float maxHp = Read<float>(hProc, playerBase + 0x008C); Write<float>(hProc, playerBase + 0x0088, maxHp);
Warning:Writing arbitrary values into game memory can cause crashes, undefined behavior, or server-side desync. The game server always maintains authoritative state in properly designed multiplayer architectures — writing client-side health to 100 will not change what the server believes your health to be. This is why server-side validation is the only real defense.

Finding the Module Base Address

To resolve static offsets (e.g., game.exe+0x01A2B3C0), you need the base address at which the game module was loaded. Use CreateToolhelp32Snapshot with TH32CS_SNAPMODULE to enumerate all modules loaded in the target process:

#include <Windows.h> #include <TlHelp32.h> #include <cstdint> #include <string> // Returns the base load address of a named module within a remote process uintptr_t GetModuleBase(DWORD pid, const std::wstring& moduleName) { HANDLE hSnap = CreateToolhelp32Snapshot( TH32CS_SNAPMODULE | TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32, // include 32-bit modules too pid ); if (hSnap == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) return 0; MODULEENTRY32W me{}; me.dwSize = sizeof(me); uintptr_t base = 0; if (Module32FirstW(hSnap, &me)) { do { if (moduleName == me.szModule) { base = reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(me.modBaseAddr); break; } } while (Module32NextW(hSnap, &me)); } CloseHandle(hSnap); return base; } // Example: resolve a static pointer stored at a fixed offset from game.exe uintptr_t gameBase = GetModuleBase(pid, L"game.exe"); // Read the entity manager pointer (a static global at moduleBase + offset) constexpr uintptr_t OFFSET_ENTITY_MGR = 0x01A2B3C0; uintptr_t entityMgr = Read<uintptr_t>(hProc, gameBase + OFFSET_ENTITY_MGR); // Follow the pointer chain to the local player uintptr_t localPlayer = Read<uintptr_t>(hProc, entityMgr + 0x0); localPlayer = Read<uintptr_t>(hProc, localPlayer + 0x58);

Note that TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32 is needed to see 32-bit modules from a 64-bit snapshot process. Omitting it causes Module32FirstW to miss modules in WoW64 games.

Building a Simple Read Loop

Putting it all together, a tool typically runs in a loop — resolving pointers each iteration (since game objects are reallocated between rounds) and sleeping between reads to avoid hammering the kernel with unnecessary RPM calls. Here is a minimal but complete example:

#include <Windows.h> #include <TlHelp32.h> #include <cstdint> #include <cstdio> #include <thread> #include <chrono> // ── Forward declarations (implementations shown in earlier sections) ─────── DWORD GetProcessId(const std::wstring& name); HANDLE OpenGameProcess(DWORD pid); uintptr_t GetModuleBase(DWORD pid, const std::wstring& mod); template <typename T> T Read (HANDLE h, uintptr_t a); template <typename T> bool Write(HANDLE h, uintptr_t a, const T& v); struct Vec3 { float x, y, z; }; // ── Offsets ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── namespace off { constexpr uintptr_t entityMgrPtr = 0x01A2B3C0; // module-relative static ptr constexpr uintptr_t vecOrigin = 0x0028; constexpr uintptr_t flHealth = 0x0088; constexpr uintptr_t iTeamNum = 0x0090; constexpr uintptr_t bAlive = 0x0094; } // ── Main loop ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── int main() { const std::wstring PROC_NAME = L"game.exe"; const int POLL_MS = 16; // ~60 Hz update rate HANDLE hProc = nullptr; uintptr_t modBase = 0; DWORD pid = 0; puts("[*] Waiting for game process..."); // Wait until game launches while (!(pid = GetProcessId(PROC_NAME))) std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::seconds(1)); hProc = OpenGameProcess(pid); modBase = GetModuleBase(pid, PROC_NAME); printf("[+] Attached. PID=%lu ModBase=0x%llX\n", pid, (unsigned long long)modBase); while (true) { // Re-resolve pointer chain each tick (handles game restarts / reloads) uintptr_t entityMgr = Read<uintptr_t>(hProc, modBase + off::entityMgrPtr); uintptr_t localPlayer = Read<uintptr_t>(hProc, entityMgr + 0x0); localPlayer = Read<uintptr_t>(hProc, localPlayer + 0x58); if (!localPlayer) { puts("[-] LocalPlayer not found (in menu?)"); std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500)); continue; } Vec3 pos = Read<Vec3> (hProc, localPlayer + off::vecOrigin); float health = Read<float>(hProc, localPlayer + off::flHealth); int team = Read<int> (hProc, localPlayer + off::iTeamNum); bool alive = Read<bool> (hProc, localPlayer + off::bAlive); // Clear line and print telemetry printf("\r[+] Pos=(%.1f,%.1f,%.1f) HP=%.0f Team=%d Alive=%s ", pos.x, pos.y, pos.z, health, team, alive ? "Y" : "N"); fflush(stdout); std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(POLL_MS)); } CloseHandle(hProc); return 0; }

This loop re-resolves the full pointer chain on every tick. While slightly redundant (pointers rarely change mid-game), it makes the tool robust across scene transitions, map loads, and game restarts without requiring any special handling. In a more optimized version, you would cache the resolved localPlayer pointer and only re-resolve it when a read returns zero or the process memory map changes.

Note:Compile with MSVC or MinGW targeting x64 (-m64). Link against no special libraries — onlykernel32.lib (implicit). Run as Administrator if OpenProcess fails due to insufficient privileges. The SeDebugPrivilege token privilege can be enabled programmatically for elevated access without running as admin, though this itself requires the token to already have the privilege assigned.

What Is Pattern Scanning and Why Use It?

When you reverse engineer a game and find the function that applies damage, you could hardcode its address — say 0x140A3F220. But the next game update recompiles the binary. New functions are added, the compiler reorders code, and your hardcoded address now points into the middle of a completely different function. Your mod crashes.

The insight behind pattern scanning is that while addresses change between updates, the compiled machine code of a specific function tends to be much more stable. A function's prologue — the first 15–30 bytes of its assembly — is often identical across minor patches because the compiler generates the same code from the same source. Instead of storing 0x140A3F220, you store the byte sequence 48 89 5C 24 08 57 48 83 EC 30 48 8B D9 and scan for it at runtime.

Pattern scanning is used extensively in:

  • Game trainers and mods — locating game logic without source access
  • Anti-cheat bypass research — finding integrity-checking routines
  • Instrumentation and profiling — hooking functions dynamically
  • Malware analysis — identifying code patterns across obfuscated samples

Generating a Pattern in IDA Pro and Ghidra

The goal is to find a sequence of bytes at the start (or a distinctive location) of your target function that is unique in the entire binary and unlikely to change across updates.

In IDA Pro:

  1. Navigate to the function in the disassembly view. Press F2 to enter hex view, or use View → Open Subviews → Hex Dump.
  2. Read the raw bytes of the function's first 10–20 instructions. Right-click the function start in the disassembly → Search → Text... to verify the sequence appears only once in the entire binary.
  3. Alternatively, install the findcrypt or sigmaker IDA plugin. Sigmaker automatically generates a minimal unique signature for the selected address, outputting it in CE-style (?? ?? 48 89) or code-style byte array format.

In Ghidra:

  1. Open the function in the Listing view. The byte values are shown in the second column to the left of the mnemonics.
  2. Use Search → Memory... (S) to enter your candidate byte sequence and verify it appears exactly once. Use \x?? as a wildcard.
  3. The community plugin SigMaker-Ghidra (available on GitHub) automates the process of growing a signature byte-by-byte until it is unique.
; Example function prologue (x64 fastcall) ; Address Bytes Mnemonic 140A3F220 48 89 5C 24 08 mov [rsp+8], rbx 140A3F225 57 push rdi 140A3F226 48 83 EC 30 sub rsp, 30h 140A3F22A 48 8B D9 mov rbx, rcx 140A3F22D E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? call <some_relative_address> ← relative, changes! 140A3F232 48 8B F8 mov rdi, rax Pattern (wildcarding the relative call target): "48 89 5C 24 08 57 48 83 EC 30 48 8B D9 E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 48 8B F8"

Wildcards — The ? Byte

Not all bytes in a pattern can be matched exactly. Some bytes encode relative addresses or absolute addresses that the linker fills in and that change every build. The canonical example is a relative CALL or JMP instruction:

  • E8 xx xx xx xx — CALL rel32. The 4 bytes after E8 are a signed 32-bit offset from the next instruction to the target. If any code between this call site and its target is added or removed, this offset changes. Wildcard all 4 bytes: E8 ?? ?? ?? ??.
  • 48 8D 05 xx xx xx xx — LEA rax, [rip + rel32]. RIP-relative data references similarly encode runtime-dependent offsets. Wildcard the 4-byte displacement.
  • FF 15 xx xx xx xx — CALL QWORD PTR [rip + rel32]. Indirect calls through the import table. Wildcard the 4 displacement bytes.

Instructions that are safe to match exactly include register-to-register operations, immediate values that are part of the algorithm logic (not addresses), and stack frame setup sequences. A good rule of thumb: if the byte sequence encodes an address, wildcard it; if it encodes logic, keep it.

Tip:Aim for patterns between 12 and 25 bytes. Shorter patterns risk false positives; longer patterns become brittle across updates (more bytes = more chances for the compiler to change something). Cross-reference your pattern against two or three game versions to verify stability before shipping.

Implementing a Pattern Scanner in C++

The scanner below operates on memory already mapped into the current process (e.g., an injected DLL scanning the host game). It parses an IDA-style pattern string ("48 89 5C ?? ?? 57") into a byte/mask pair, then iterates over executable memory regions using VirtualQuery.

// pattern_scanner.hpp #pragma once #include <Windows.h> #include <vector> #include <string> #include <sstream> #include <cstdint> #include <optional> struct PatternByte { uint8_t value; bool isWildcard; }; // Parse "48 89 5C ?? 08 57" into a vector of PatternByte inline std::vector<PatternByte> ParsePattern(const std::string& pattern) { std::vector<PatternByte> result; std::istringstream ss(pattern); std::string token; while (ss >> token) { PatternByte pb{}; if (token == "?" || token == "??") { pb.isWildcard = true; pb.value = 0x00; } else { pb.isWildcard = false; pb.value = static_cast<uint8_t>(std::stoul(token, nullptr, 16)); } result.push_back(pb); } return result; } // Compare bytes at 'data' against 'pattern', respecting wildcards inline bool MatchPattern(const uint8_t* data, const std::vector<PatternByte>& pattern) { for (size_t i = 0; i < pattern.size(); ++i) { if (!pattern[i].isWildcard && data[i] != pattern[i].value) return false; } return true; } // Scan a single contiguous region [base, base+size) for the pattern inline std::optional<uintptr_t> ScanRegion(const uint8_t* base, size_t regionSize, const std::vector<PatternByte>& pattern) { if (pattern.empty() || regionSize < pattern.size()) return std::nullopt; const size_t scanEnd = regionSize - pattern.size(); for (size_t offset = 0; offset <= scanEnd; ++offset) { if (MatchPattern(base + offset, pattern)) return reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(base + offset); } return std::nullopt; } // Scan all committed, executable memory regions of the current process // for the given IDA-style pattern string. Returns the first match. inline std::optional<uintptr_t> PatternScan(const std::string& patternStr) { auto pattern = ParsePattern(patternStr); if (pattern.empty()) return std::nullopt; MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION mbi{}; uintptr_t address = 0; while (VirtualQuery(reinterpret_cast<LPCVOID>(address), &mbi, sizeof(mbi)) == sizeof(mbi)) { // Only scan committed, executable regions (skip guard pages, no-access) bool isCommitted = (mbi.State == MEM_COMMIT); bool isExecutable = (mbi.Protect & (PAGE_EXECUTE | PAGE_EXECUTE_READ | PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE | PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY)); bool notGuard = !(mbi.Protect & PAGE_GUARD); if (isCommitted && isExecutable && notGuard) { auto match = ScanRegion( reinterpret_cast<const uint8_t*>(mbi.BaseAddress), mbi.RegionSize, pattern ); if (match.has_value()) return match; } // Advance to the next region; guard against overflow uintptr_t next = reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(mbi.BaseAddress) + mbi.RegionSize; if (next <= address) break; // wrapped around address = next; } return std::nullopt; } // ── Usage example ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // auto result = PatternScan("48 89 5C 24 08 57 48 83 EC 30 48 8B D9 E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 48 8B F8"); // if (result) { // uintptr_t funcAddr = *result; // // resolve relative offset if needed: // // uintptr_t target = funcAddr + 14 + 4 + *reinterpret_cast<int32_t*>(funcAddr + 14); // }

The scanner runs in O(n·m) time where n is the total committed executable bytes and m is pattern length. For a 100 MB game binary this takes roughly 50–200ms on modern hardware — acceptable for one-time initialization but too slow to call per-frame.

Using VirtualQuery to Enumerate Memory Regions

VirtualQuery (or VirtualQueryEx for external processes) fills a MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION structure describing the region that starts at or contains the queried address. Key fields:

typedef struct _MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION { PVOID BaseAddress; // start of this region PVOID AllocationBase; // base of the VirtualAlloc that created it DWORD AllocationProtect; // protection at allocation time SIZE_T RegionSize; // byte size of this region (contiguous same-attribute pages) DWORD State; // MEM_COMMIT | MEM_FREE | MEM_RESERVE DWORD Protect; // current protection flags (PAGE_EXECUTE_READ, etc.) DWORD Type; // MEM_IMAGE | MEM_MAPPED | MEM_PRIVATE } MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION; // To restrict scanning to a specific module only (much faster): // 1. Get module base: GetModuleHandleA("game.exe") // 2. Read PE header to get SizeOfImage // 3. Call ScanRegion() on [moduleBase, moduleBase + SizeOfImage] HMODULE hMod = GetModuleHandleA(nullptr); // nullptr = main EXE MODULEINFO mi{}; GetModuleInformation(GetCurrentProcess(), hMod, &mi, sizeof(mi)); // mi.lpBaseOfDll = base address // mi.SizeOfImage = total mapped size

Restricting the scan to a known module's image region (Type == MEM_IMAGE) dramatically reduces scan time and false positives, since you are only searching compiled code pages rather than heap allocations or stack memory. For a 64 MB game EXE, the scan typically completes in under 10ms.

Caching Patterns and Handling Update Breakage

Scanning on every launch adds startup latency. A simple caching strategy stores the resolved address alongside a game build identifier (e.g., a hash of the EXE or the PE TimeDateStamp field) in a local config file. On next launch, if the build ID matches, use the cached offset directly; otherwise re-scan and update the cache.

// cache.hpp — simplified offset cache #pragma once #include <Windows.h> #include <fstream> #include <unordered_map> #include <string> // Read PE TimeDateStamp as a simple build fingerprint inline uint32_t GetModuleTimestamp(HMODULE hMod) { auto* dosHdr = reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_DOS_HEADER*>(hMod); auto* ntHdr = reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_NT_HEADERS*>( reinterpret_cast<uint8_t*>(hMod) + dosHdr->e_lfanew); return ntHdr->FileHeader.TimeDateStamp; } struct OffsetCache { uint32_t buildStamp = 0; std::unordered_map<std::string, uintptr_t> offsets; void Load(const std::string& path) { /* read JSON/INI */ } void Save(const std::string& path) { /* write JSON/INI */ } uintptr_t Resolve(const std::string& name, const std::string& pattern, HMODULE hMod) { uint32_t stamp = GetModuleTimestamp(hMod); if (buildStamp != stamp) { offsets.clear(); // stale cache — invalidate everything buildStamp = stamp; } auto it = offsets.find(name); if (it != offsets.end()) return it->second; // cache hit // Cache miss — scan auto base = reinterpret_cast<uintptr_t>(hMod); auto result = PatternScan(pattern); // scoped to module for speed if (!result) return 0; uintptr_t offset = *result - base; // store as relative offset offsets[name] = offset; return *result; } };

When a game update does break a pattern, the fallback strategy is to have multiple candidate patterns for the same target — ordered from most to least specific — and try them in sequence. Automated CI pipelines in larger modding communities download new game builds, run the pattern list, and report which signatures need updating before the community is even aware the game patched.

Advanced Technique:Instead of matching at the function entry point, match at a distinctive instruction deep inside the function body, then walk backward to the nearest CC CC CC (INT3 padding) or 90 90 90 (NOP padding) alignment sequence to find the true function start. This works even when the prologue changes but the body is stable.

1. What Is pymem?

pymem is a Python library that exposes the Windows ReadProcessMemory, WriteProcessMemory, and related memory management APIs through ctypes bindings. It lets you open a handle to any running process, scan its virtual address space, read typed values, and write changes — all from Python without writing a single line of C++.

Its primary use cases in game security research are:

  • Rapid prototyping — Verify that an offset you found in Cheat Engine is correct before hardcoding it into a C++ project. Python's interactive REPL makes this very fast.
  • Simple automation — Build lightweight bots that react to memory-read values (health, position, cooldowns) without a full C++ DLL.
  • Research tooling — Write memory dumpers, structure mappers, and analysis scripts that process game data offline.

Internally, pymem calls OpenProcess with the PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS flag to obtain a handle, then delegates to the Win32 ReadProcessMemory / WriteProcessMemory functions. It also wraps CreateToolhelp32Snapshot for module enumeration, which is how it resolves module base addresses.

2. Installation

pymem is available on PyPI. It requires Python 3.7+ and Windows (it uses Win32 APIs directly and will not work on Linux or macOS). No native compilation is required — it is pure Python.

# Install pymem pip install pymem # Optional but recommended for struct unpacking pip install pywin32 # Verify the install python -c "import pymem; print(pymem.__version__)" # Expected: 1.x.x

Run your Python scripts with Administrator privileges. Without elevation, OpenProcess will fail with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (5) when trying to attach to most game processes, which run in a higher integrity level or have protected process flags.

Note:Use a virtual environment (python -m venv venv) to isolate pymem from your system Python. This prevents version conflicts when working across multiple research projects.

3. Attaching to a Process by Name

The entry point for any pymem session is the Pymem class. Instantiating it with a process name searches the running process list, finds the PID, and opens a handle automatically.

import pymem import pymem.process # Attach by process name (must be running) pm = pymem.Pymem("game.exe") # The process ID and handle are now available: print(f"PID: {pm.process_id}") print(f"Handle: {pm.process_handle}") # Get the base address of the main module (game.exe itself): base = pymem.process.module_from_name(pm.process_handle, "game.exe").lpBaseOfDll print(f"Base address: {hex(base)}") # You can also get any loaded module's base: engine_base = pymem.process.module_from_name(pm.process_handle, "engine.dll").lpBaseOfDll print(f"engine.dll base: {hex(engine_base)}")

If the process is not running, pymem raises pymem.exception.ProcessNotFound. Wrap the constructor in a try/except during development to handle this gracefully:

import pymem from pymem.exception import ProcessNotFound try: pm = pymem.Pymem("game.exe") except ProcessNotFound: print("game.exe is not running. Launch the game first.") raise SystemExit(1)

4. Reading Basic Types

pymem provides convenience methods for reading common primitive types directly from a memory address. Under the hood each of these calls ReadProcessMemory and unpacks the raw bytes using Python's struct module.

import pymem import struct pm = pymem.Pymem("game.exe") # --- Reading integers --- # Read a 4-byte signed integer (int32) from an absolute address health_addr = 0x1A2B3C40 health = pm.read_int(health_addr) print(f"Health: {health}") # Read an 8-byte integer (int64 / QWORD) score = pm.read_longlong(0x1A2B3C50) # Read a 4-byte unsigned integer (DWORD) flags = pm.read_uint(0x1A2B3C60) # --- Reading floats --- # Read a single-precision 4-byte float (the most common in games) speed = pm.read_float(0x1A2B3C70) print(f"Speed: {speed:.2f}") # --- Reading booleans --- # Games typically store bools as a single byte (0 or 1) is_grounded_byte = pm.read_bytes(0x1A2B3C80, 1) is_grounded = bool(is_grounded_byte[0]) # --- Reading a Vec3 (3D position vector) --- # A Vec3 is 3 consecutive floats: X at addr, Y at addr+4, Z at addr+8 def read_vec3(pm: pymem.Pymem, address: int) -> tuple[float, float, float]: raw = pm.read_bytes(address, 12) # 3 floats * 4 bytes each = 12 bytes x, y, z = struct.unpack("fff", raw) return (x, y, z) pos_addr = 0x1A2B3C90 pos = read_vec3(pm, pos_addr) print(f"Player position: X={pos[0]:.2f}, Y={pos[1]:.2f}, Z={pos[2]:.2f}")

The full list of pymem read methods includes: read_int, read_uint, read_short, read_ushort, read_long, read_ulong, read_longlong, read_ulonglong, read_float, read_double, read_bool, read_char, read_string, and read_bytes. For any type not directly supported, use read_bytes(addr, n) and unpack manually with struct.unpack.

5. Pointer Chain Resolution

Games allocate most of their game-state objects on the heap at addresses that change every time the process starts (due to ASLR and heap randomization). A pointer chain is a sequence of memory reads starting from a stable base address (usually a static offset from the module base) that navigates through a series of pointers — each read gives you the address for the next step — until you reach the final value.

Cheat Engine's pointer scanner finds these chains for you. The chain is typically represented as: [[[base + 0x1A0] + 0x48] + 0x18] + 0xC — meaning a 4-step chain with 3 dereferences and a final offset.

import pymem import pymem.process def resolve_pointer_chain( pm: pymem.Pymem, base_address: int, offsets: list[int] ) -> int: """ Resolve a multi-level pointer chain. Args: pm: Pymem instance attached to the target process. base_address: The starting static address (e.g., module base + static offset). offsets: List of offsets to dereference in order. The last offset is added but NOT dereferenced — it gives the final address of the target value. Returns: The final resolved address of the target value. Example chain from Cheat Engine: [[[game.exe + 0x01A2B3C0] + 0x48] + 0x18] + 0x0C base_address = module_base + 0x01A2B3C0 offsets = [0x48, 0x18, 0x0C] """ addr = pm.read_longlong(base_address) # First dereference from static base for offset in offsets[:-1]: # All offsets except the last addr = pm.read_longlong(addr + offset) return addr + offsets[-1] # Final offset — the value's address # Example usage: pm = pymem.Pymem("game.exe") module_base = pymem.process.module_from_name( pm.process_handle, "game.exe" ).lpBaseOfDll # Pointer chain found with Cheat Engine: # game.exe + 0x01A2B3C0 → +0x48 → +0x18 → +0x0C (target: player health, int32) STATIC_OFFSET = 0x01A2B3C0 OFFSETS = [0x48, 0x18, 0x0C] try: health_addr = resolve_pointer_chain( pm, module_base + STATIC_OFFSET, OFFSETS ) health = pm.read_int(health_addr) print(f"Player health: {health}") except Exception as e: # A read_longlong will throw if any intermediate pointer is NULL or invalid print(f"Pointer chain broken — game may not be in a valid state: {e}") # --- Writing through the pointer chain --- def write_via_chain(pm, base_address, offsets, value_writer, value): addr = resolve_pointer_chain(pm, base_address, offsets) value_writer(addr, value) # Set health to 100: write_via_chain(pm, module_base + STATIC_OFFSET, OFFSETS, pm.write_int, 100)
Note:On a 64-bit process, always use read_longlong (8 bytes) to dereference pointers — not read_int (4 bytes). Using the wrong size will truncate the pointer and produce an invalid address. On legacy 32-bit games, use read_uint (4 bytes) for pointer reads.

6. Limitations vs. C++

pymem is a great prototyping tool but has fundamental limitations compared to a proper C++ DLL injected into the game process. Understanding these tradeoffs helps you decide when Python is sufficient and when to graduate to C++.

  • Performance: Every ReadProcessMemory call crosses a process boundary — it is a kernel transition. Python adds interpreter overhead on top of this. A tight Python loop reading memory 60 times/second will consume noticeably more CPU than an equivalent C++ DLL running in-process, where a memory read is a single pointer dereference with no syscall overhead.
  • Anti-cheat detection: External memory reading (a separate .exe or script calling ReadProcessMemory on the game) is one of the most-watched patterns by kernel-level anti-cheat software. A Python process with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS on a game handle is trivially detectable. C++ code injected as a DLL runs inside the game's address space and has a smaller detection surface — though it is by no means undetectable.
  • No kernel access: pymem operates entirely in user mode. It cannot hook kernel callbacks, read kernel-mode data structures (EPROCESS, KTHREAD), manipulate driver objects, or bypass kernel-mode anti-cheat protections that operate at ring 0. Any research involving kernel-level techniques requires a Windows driver (WDM/WDF) written in C.
  • No code injection: pymem can write bytes to memory, but it cannot easily allocate remote executable memory, write shellcode, or call game functions — tasks that require VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread or equivalent techniques, which are much simpler to orchestrate from C++.
  • Windows-only: The underlying Win32 APIs are Windows-specific. pymem will not run on Linux (Proton/Wine environments present a different memory API surface) or macOS.
When to use pymem vs. C++:Use pymem when you are exploring an unknown game and validating offsets, or building a one-off research script. Switch to C++ when you need in-process speed, code hooking (trampolines, vtable patches), or anything requiring more than basic memory read/write from outside the process.

Introduction to x64dbg

x64dbg (x64dbg.com) is open source under the GPL license and maintained actively on GitHub. It provides a multi-pane UI with: CPU disassembly view, register window, stack view, memory dump, and a log/command console. Compared to its predecessor OllyDbg, it offers:

  • Native 64-bit support — OllyDbg was 32-bit only. x64dbg ships as paired binaries (x32dbg.exe / x64dbg.exe) and the launcher auto-selects based on target architecture.
  • Plugin API — a rich C++ plugin SDK. Widely-used plugins include ScyllaHide (anti-anti-debug), xAnalyzer (auto-analysis and annotation), and ret-sync (bidirectional sync with IDA/Ghidra).
  • Integrated scripting — a built-in scripting language (x64dbg Script) and Lua support via plugins allow you to automate repetitive analysis tasks.
  • Symbol resolution — downloads PDB symbols from Microsoft Symbol Server and applies them to Windows system DLLs, making call stacks and API calls immediately readable.
  • Conditional and trace breakpoints — break only when a register or memory value matches a condition, or log-and-continue to trace execution without halting.

Attaching vs Opening an Executable

x64dbg offers two entry modes, each suited to different research scenarios:

  • File → Open (F3) — x64dbg launches the target executable itself, breaking at the process entry point (or the TLS callbacks if present). This is the cleanest way to study initialization code, anti-debug routines that run early in startup, or unpacking stubs. The game's anti-cheat may not yet be active at this stage.
  • File → Attach (Alt+A) — attaches to an already-running process. Ideal when you need the game fully loaded and a play session active (so your target data — e.g., a live health value — is present in memory). The debugger interrupts all threads on attach; press Run (F9) to resume.

After attaching, x64dbg populates the Symbols tab with all loaded modules. Expand the game's main module to see exported functions (if any) and referenced imports. Most game binaries strip symbols, so you will see raw addresses — but Windows API imports in the Import Address Table (IAT) remain readable and are extremely useful anchors.

Warning:Attaching a debugger is detectable. Games with active anti-cheat (EAC, BattlEye, Vanguard) instrumentNtQueryInformationProcess, check the BeingDebugged flag in the PEB, and scan for debug registers. Use ScyllaHide or conduct research exclusively in offline / LAN modes.

Setting Breakpoints — Software and Hardware

Breakpoints are the primary mechanism for catching execution at a point of interest. x64dbg supports two fundamentally different kinds:

Software Breakpoints (INT3)

The debugger replaces the first byte of the target instruction with 0xCC (the INT3 opcode). When the CPU executes it, an exception fires and the debugger resumes control. Set one by clicking the left gutter of the CPU view or pressing F2 on a selected instruction. Software BPs are detectable — the game can scan its own code pages for 0xCC bytes.

Hardware Breakpoints (DR0–DR3)

The x86 architecture provides four debug registers (DR0–DR3) that can trigger a debug exception when a specific address is executed, read, or written — without modifying any code bytes. This makes them ideal for catching the exact instruction that reads or writes a game value:

  1. Locate the memory address of the health float (via Cheat Engine, as covered in the ReClass guide).
  2. In x64dbg's Memory Map tab, right-click the address (or use Follow in Dumpfrom the CPU view), then Breakpoint → Hardware, on access (4 bytes).
  3. Return to the game and trigger a health change. The debugger will break at the exact instruction that wrote the new health value — this is the code path you want to analyze.
; Typical result when breaking on health write: ; x64dbg breaks here — call stack will show the combat damage function above 0x7FF63A1B2C40 movss [rcx+88h], xmm0 ; store new health (float) into entity+0x88 ; rcx = PlayerEntity base address ; xmm0 = computed new health value (e.g., 75.0) 0x7FF63A1B2C48 movss xmm1, [rcx+8Ch] ; load maxHealth for clamping 0x7FF63A1B2C4D comiss xmm0, xmm1 ; compare health <= maxHealth 0x7FF63A1B2C50 jbe short 0x7FF63A1B2C58

The offset 0x88 in the instruction above directly confirms the flHealth offset within the entity structure — exactly what ReClass.NET would show visually.

Reading the Disassembly

Once execution is paused at a breakpoint, the CPU view shows the surrounding disassembly. Recognizing common compiler patterns accelerates analysis significantly.

Function Prologues

MSVC and Clang on x64 Windows always emit a standard prologue. When you see this pattern, you are at the top of a function:

; Standard x64 MSVC function prologue sub rsp, 48h ; reserve shadow space + locals on stack mov [rsp+20h], rbx ; save non-volatile registers mov [rsp+28h], rsi mov [rsp+30h], rdi ; ... function body follows

Calling Conventions

x64 Windows uses the Microsoft ABI: first four integer/pointer arguments in RCX, RDX, R8, R9; first four float arguments in XMM0–XMM3; additional args on the stack. For C++ member functions, RCX is always this. This means if you break inside a method and see [rcx+88h], you know RCX holds the object pointer and 0x88 is the field offset.

Identifying Loops

; Entity list iteration — common pattern in game update functions xor ecx, ecx ; i = 0 .loop_start: cmp ecx, [rbx+entityCount]; compare i with entity count jge .loop_end ; if i >= count, exit loop movsxd rax, ecx lea rax, [rax+rax*2] ; rax = i * 3 (stride trick) shl rax, 4 ; rax = i * 48 (entity stride = 0x30) add rax, [rbx+entityBase] ; rax = &entityList[i] ; ... process entity at rax inc ecx jmp .loop_start .loop_end:

Memory Map and Pattern / String Search

x64dbg's Memory Map tab lists every virtual memory region: its base address, size, page protection flags (ERW), memory type (MEM_IMAGE, MEM_PRIVATE), and the module it belongs to. This is essential for:

  • Identifying code vs data sections — MEM_IMAGE + PAGE_EXECUTE_READ regions are code;MEM_PRIVATE + PAGE_READWRITE are heap/stack.
  • String searching — Right-click any module entry → Search for Pattern, or use the command console: findallmem game.exe:, "Player". Games often embed debug strings like"DamagePlayer" or "SetHealth" that directly lead you to the relevant function.
  • Byte pattern (signature) scanning — use the References → Search for dialog or the findall command with a hex pattern to locate a function across updates without knowing its address: findall game.exe:, "F3 0F 11 41 88" (the movss [rcx+88h], xmm0 encoding).

String references are one of the most reliable entry points into unfamiliar code. Once you find the string reference, right-click → Follow in Disassembler → scroll up to see which function uses it and trace its call chain upward.

Scripting with x64dbg Script Language

x64dbg has a built-in scripting language accessible via File → Run Script or the command console. Scripts use a line-oriented syntax with labels, conditionals, and a rich command set. Below is a practical script that automates finding which code path sets the player's health, by setting a hardware breakpoint and logging every write with its context:

// x64dbg Script: trace_health_writes.txt // Usage: File -> Run Script -> select this file // Prerequisites: RCX must already point to a known PlayerEntity // Set $healthAddr manually before running, or resolve via expression // ── Step 1: Resolve health field address ───────────────────────────────── // Assume rcx holds a known player entity base — capture it first via BP var $entityBase var $healthAddr // Read rcx value at current EIP context (after a manual BP on entity ctor) $entityBase = rcx $healthAddr = $entityBase + 0x88 // flHealth offset msg "Health address: {$healthAddr}" // ── Step 2: Set hardware breakpoint (write, 4 bytes) ───────────────────── bphws $healthAddr, "w", 4 // ── Step 3: Set a conditional log-and-continue trace ───────────────────── // bplog logs but does not stop execution — "hit" continues automatically bplog $healthAddr, "HEALTH WRITE — new value: {[{$healthAddr}]:f} caller={cip}" // ── Step 4: Resume execution ────────────────────────────────────────────── run // The log tab will accumulate every write to health with the calling address. // Stop manually (Pause) after triggering several damage events, then review // the log to find the canonical SetHealth function address.

In the script above, bphws sets a hardware write breakpoint, and bplog configures it as a trace (log-only, no halt). The expression [{$healthAddr}]:f dereferences the health address and formats the result as a 32-bit float. After triggering several damage events in-game, your log will contain lines like:

HEALTH WRITE — new value: 75.000000 caller=7FF63A1B2C40 HEALTH WRITE — new value: 50.000000 caller=7FF63A1B2C40 HEALTH WRITE — new value: 100.000000 caller=7FF63A1B2E90 ; <-- different caller, likely heal

The two distinct callers immediately reveal separate "take damage" and "receive healing" code paths — a level of insight that would take significantly longer to reach manually.

Note:For more complex automation, consider the Lua plugin (LuaScript) or the Python plugin (x64dbgpy), both available in the x64dbg plugin repository. They expose the full debugger API and allow integration with external analysis pipelines.
