Categories of Anti-Cheat

Anti-cheat systems are commonly classified along two axes: where detection runs (client vs server) andwhat privilege level the client component operates at.

  • User-mode client-side (Ring 3) — runs as a normal application process or loaded DLL within the game process. Can inspect other user-space processes, read the file system, and query Windows APIs. Limited by the fact that sophisticated tools can operate at a lower ring level and remain invisible. Examples: early VAC versions, PunkBuster era.
  • Kernel-mode client-side (Ring 0) — installs a kernel driver (.sys file) that operates with full OS privileges. Can inspect any process, hook system calls, access hardware-level features, and detect tampering that user-mode tools cannot see. The modern standard for competitive games. Examples: Riot Vanguard, FACEIT AC, BattlEye (current), EAC (kernel mode available).
  • Server-side — validation logic runs on the authoritative game server. Analyzes player statistics, trajectory data, shot patterns, and physics consistency. Cannot be bypassed by any client modification. The only reliable long-term defense but requires significant engineering investment. Examples: Valve Overwatch, statistical ban systems.
  • Hybrid — all modern serious anti-cheat systems use a combination: kernel-mode client component for immediate detection + server-side analysis for statistical validation + delayed ban waves to prevent cheaters from pinpointing what triggered detection.

EasyAntiCheat (EAC) — Detection Mechanisms

EasyAntiCheat (now owned by Epic Games) is one of the most widely deployed anti-cheat systems, used in titles including Fortnite, Apex Legends, Rust, and hundreds of others. Its architecture has evolved significantly from its early user-mode-only implementation.

Process and Module Scanning

EAC enumerates the running process list and loaded module list of the game process using the same Toolhelp32 and PSAPI APIs available to user-mode code. It checks loaded modules against an allowlist and flags any unrecognized DLL injected into the game's address space. It also inspects process names and window titles of other running applications against a blocklist of known cheat tools and debuggers.

Memory Integrity Verification

EAC periodically checksums the game's own code sections (.text segment of the main executable and key DLLs) to detect runtime code patching. Any byte modification — including INT3 software breakpoints — will trigger a mismatch. The checksums are sent to EAC's cloud backend for server-side verification, preventing simple checksum spoofing.

Driver Signing and Kernel Mode

Modern EAC optionally deploys a kernel-mode driver (EasyAntiCheat.sys). This driver is WHQL-signed and requires Windows Driver Signature Enforcement to be active. It monitors handle access to the game process from external processes — specifically watching for PROCESS_VM_READ or PROCESS_VM_WRITE access granted to non-system processes. From kernel mode, it can also enumerate loaded kernel drivers and detect unauthorized drivers that may be providing privileged memory access.

// EAC kernel driver conceptually instruments ObRegisterCallbacks // to monitor process handle creation — something like: OB_PREOP_CALLBACK_STATUS HandleCallback( PVOID RegistrationContext, POB_PRE_OPERATION_INFORMATION OpInfo) { if (OpInfo->ObjectType == *PsProcessType) { PEPROCESS targetProcess = (PEPROCESS)OpInfo->Object; // If someone is opening a handle to the game process... if (targetProcess == g_GameProcess) { // Strip VM read/write access from the requested access mask // unless the requester is a trusted system process OpInfo->Parameters->CreateHandleInformation.DesiredAccess &= ~(PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_VM_WRITE); } } return OB_PREOP_SUCCESS; }

BattlEye — Architecture and Detection

BattlEye (BE) is used in Escape from Tarkov, DayZ, Rainbow Six Siege, PUBG, and many others. It is known for aggressive kernel-mode detection and has been publicly documented by researchers and the BE team itself.

Ring-0 Driver and Historical SSDT Hooks

In earlier versions, BattlEye's kernel driver hooked the System Service Descriptor Table (SSDT) — a table of pointers to native NT system call handlers. By replacing entries for calls like NtOpenProcess, NtReadVirtualMemory, and NtWriteVirtualMemory, BE could intercept any attempt to access the game process from user mode and block or log the call. Microsoft's introduction of PatchGuard (Kernel Patch Protection, KPP) in x64 Windows made SSDT hooking incompatible with modern systems — PatchGuard periodically verifies the integrity of the SSDT and BSODs the system if modifications are detected.

Modern PatchGuard-Aware Approach

Current BattlEye uses the documented ObRegisterCallbacks API (same as EAC above) rather than SSDT hooks, making it fully PatchGuard-compatible. It also uses PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine to be notified every time any image (driver, DLL, executable) is loaded system-wide — this catches driver-based cheating tools before they can establish themselves. Additionally, BE scans physical memory for known cheat signatures using mapped kernel memory and MmMapIoSpace-style operations.

Communication and Updates

BattlEye employs a dynamic update mechanism — its core scanning logic is downloaded in encrypted, obfuscated form at game startup and changes frequently. This makes static signature-based evasion quickly obsolete. The driver maintains a persistent encrypted channel to BE's cloud backend for log submission and scan data upload.

VAC — Steam's Approach

Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC) is distinct from EAC and BattlEye in philosophy: it deliberately prioritizes false-positive avoidance over instant detection. VAC operates entirely in user mode and is known for several characteristic behaviors documented through Valve's own statements and security research.

Offline / Asynchronous Scanning

VAC does not rely on real-time kernel monitoring. Instead, it runs periodic scans of the game process and the system during play sessions. Scan modules are downloaded from Valve's content delivery network, executed, and the results are sent to Valve's backend servers for analysis — the client never knows which specific checks are being run at any given time.

Hash-Based Detection

VAC's most well-documented detection mechanism is hash-based: it computes cryptographic hashes of DLLs and executables on disk and in memory. Known cheat binaries and game modification libraries are matched against a server-side database of malicious hashes. Because this operates on file hashes, trivial recompilation or binary patching of a cheat can sometimes evade it — Valve counters this by maintaining a large and continuously updated hash database.

Delayed Bans

VAC is famous for "ban waves" — detections are logged but bans are not issued immediately. Valve has historically issued bans weeks or months after initial detection. This serves multiple purposes: it prevents cheaters from determining exactly which action triggered detection, it allows Valve to accumulate enough evidence to ensure confidence, and it disrupts the cheat-development feedback loop (cheaters cannot quickly test whether a modification evades detection).

Note:VAC bans are permanent and tied to the Steam account, not hardware. A VAC ban restricts the account from playing VAC-secured servers in the banned game. Valve does not communicate specific reasons for bans, which is intentional — revealing detection specifics would allow evasion.

Kernel-Level Anti-Cheat — Vanguard and FACEIT

Riot Vanguard (used in Valorant, League of Legends) and FACEIT Anti-Cheat represent the most invasive category of anti-cheat currently deployed to consumer systems. They run kernel drivers that start at Windows boot — not only when the game is running — giving them the maximum possible vantage point.

Why Ring-0?

The fundamental reason for kernel-mode operation is that any user-mode anti-cheat can be defeated by a kernel-mode cheat. A driver running at ring-0 can hide processes from the task manager, make DLLs invisible to module enumeration APIs, and intercept memory reads at the hardware page-table level using techniques like DKOM (Direct Kernel Object Manipulation). Running the anti-cheat in the kernel places it on equal footing with the most sophisticated attack tools.

Vanguard's Boot-Time Driver

vgk.sys (Vanguard's kernel component) starts as a boot-start driver — it is initialized by Windows during the kernel boot phase, before any user session begins. This means it is active before any cheat tool could load. It uses ObRegisterCallbacks to protect Valorant's process, monitors for unsigned or improperly signed drivers, and hooks into Windows security callbacks to detect kernel exploits. Vanguard requires Secure Boot and TPM 2.0 (enforced in Windows 11) to prevent tampering with the boot chain itself — a bootkit could otherwise load before vgk.sys.

TPM and Secure Boot Requirements

Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and Secure Boot together create a hardware root of trust. Secure Boot ensures only Microsoft-signed bootloaders execute, preventing bootkits. TPM can be used for hardware fingerprinting — binding a ban to the physical machine rather than just an account. Riot's requirement for these features in Valorant was controversial but reflects a genuine security rationale: without a hardware root of trust, a sufficiently motivated attacker can bypass any software-only protection by booting a modified OS.

// Conceptual: kernel driver checking for unsigned drivers using // PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine callback VOID ImageLoadCallback( PUNICODE_STRING FullImageName, HANDLE ProcessId, // 0 = kernel driver load PIMAGE_INFO ImageInfo) { if (ProcessId == 0) { // A kernel driver is loading // Verify the image has a valid Microsoft WHQL or EV code signing cert NTSTATUS status = VerifyImageSignature(FullImageName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) { // Log the unsigned driver load attempt LogSuspiciousDriver(FullImageName, ImageInfo->ImageBase); // Anti-cheat may choose to block the game from launching, // or flag the session for server-side review } } }

Server-Side Validation — The Real Defense

The security research community broadly agrees on a fundamental principle: client-side anti-cheat alone is never sufficient. Because the cheat operator controls the physical hardware and operating system, any client-side protection can theoretically be defeated given enough time and resources. The only architecturally sound defense is server-side authoritative validation.

What Server-Side Validation Means in Practice

  • Authoritative physics — the server computes all game state. Clients submit inputs (key presses, mouse movement) and the server determines outcomes. A client reporting "I shot and hit" is meaningless — the server independently validates whether the shot trajectory was geometrically possible given both players' positions.
  • Statistical anomaly detection — the server logs headshot rates, reaction times, tracking smoothness, and pre-fire patterns. Machine learning models identify statistical distributions inconsistent with human performance. This catches subtle aim assistance that pixel-perfect pattern matching cannot.
  • Rate limiting and input validation — the server rejects inputs that are physically impossible (movement faster than max speed, actions faster than frame rate, etc.). Writing a speed value into client memory has no effect if the server rejects the resulting movement as impossible.
  • Replay analysis — server-recorded replays can be analyzed offline using automated tools and human review (Valve's Overwatch system) to flag suspicious sessions after the fact.

The most technically sophisticated cheats — those that operate entirely in kernel space, use DMA (Direct Memory Access) hardware to read game memory from a second PC without touching the game process, or run AI-based visual input processing via external GPU capture — are fundamentally immune to any client-side detection. A DMA-based setup has no footprint on the target machine whatsoever. Against these threats, server-side behavioral analysis is the only viable defense layer.

Key Takeaway:The security engineering lesson from studying anti-cheat systems is that defense-in-depth matters. Kernel-mode client anti-cheat catches the broad population of script-kiddie level tools. Statistical server-side analysis catches sophisticated actors. Neither layer alone is sufficient — both are necessary, and they complement each other by operating on different parts of the threat surface.

What Is DLL Injection?

When Windows loads a DLL normally, the target process calls LoadLibrary("mylib.dll") itself — it is an explicit, consensual load. DLL injection means a second process causes the DLL to appear in the first process's address space without a direct LoadLibrary call in the target binary. Once loaded, the injected DLL's code runs inside the target process with the same privileges and memory access as the target itself.

From a memory layout perspective, injecting a DLL is equivalent to the target process loading it voluntarily: the PE file is mapped into a region of the target's virtual address space, imports are resolved, relocations are applied, and DllMain is called with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH. The DLL's code can then read and write any memory the process owns, call any function in any loaded module, and create threads that execute indefinitely.

  • Overlays: Steam, Discord, GeForce Experience all inject DLLs to render UI on top of the game's DirectX/Vulkan swap chain.
  • Debugging & profiling: Tools like Intel VTune and RenderDoc inject to intercept graphics API calls.
  • Accessibility: Screen readers inject into browsers to read DOM content that Win32 accessibility APIs cannot reach.
  • Game modding: Script extenders (Skyrim Script Extender, etc.) inject to add new scripting capabilities to games.
  • Security research: Studying how anti-cheat software works, building defenses, and understanding attack surfaces.

LoadLibrary Injection — The Classic Technique

The most widely understood injection method uses CreateRemoteThread to execute LoadLibraryA (or LoadLibraryW) inside the target process. The key insight is that kernel32.dll is loaded at the same base address in every user-mode process on a given Windows session (thanks to ASLR being module-level, not per-process for system DLLs in most configurations). This means the address of LoadLibraryA you read from your own process is valid in the target process too.

Step-by-step walkthrough:

  1. Open the target process with sufficient access rights (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS or at minimum PROCESS_VM_WRITE | PROCESS_VM_OPERATION | PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD).
  2. Allocate memory in the target for the DLL path string using VirtualAllocEx. The path must be the absolute filesystem path to the DLL you want loaded.
  3. Write the DLL path into the allocated region with WriteProcessMemory.
  4. Resolve LoadLibraryA in your own process via GetProcAddress(GetModuleHandleA("kernel32.dll"), "LoadLibraryA").
  5. Create a remote thread with CreateRemoteThread, setting the thread start address to LoadLibraryA and the parameter to the remote memory pointer holding the DLL path. Windows will call LoadLibraryA(remotePath) in the context of the target process.
  6. Wait and clean up: WaitForSingleObject on the thread handle, then VirtualFreeEx the allocated path memory.
// LoadLibrary injection // Requires: target process PID, absolute path to DLL bool InjectDLL(DWORD targetPid, const char* dllPath) { // Step 1: open target process HANDLE hProc = OpenProcess( PROCESS_VM_WRITE | PROCESS_VM_OPERATION | PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD, FALSE, targetPid); if (!hProc) return false; size_t pathLen = strlen(dllPath) + 1; // Step 2: allocate space for the path string inside the target LPVOID remoteMem = VirtualAllocEx( hProc, nullptr, pathLen, MEM_COMMIT | MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_READWRITE); if (!remoteMem) { CloseHandle(hProc); return false; } // Step 3: write the DLL path into that remote allocation if (!WriteProcessMemory(hProc, remoteMem, dllPath, pathLen, nullptr)) { VirtualFreeEx(hProc, remoteMem, 0, MEM_RELEASE); CloseHandle(hProc); return false; } // Step 4: resolve LoadLibraryA — same address in every process FARPROC loadLib = GetProcAddress( GetModuleHandleA("kernel32.dll"), "LoadLibraryA"); // Step 5: create a remote thread that calls LoadLibraryA(remoteMem) HANDLE hThread = CreateRemoteThread( hProc, nullptr, 0, reinterpret_cast<LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE>(loadLib), remoteMem, 0, nullptr); if (!hThread) { VirtualFreeEx(hProc, remoteMem, 0, MEM_RELEASE); CloseHandle(hProc); return false; } // Step 6: wait for LoadLibraryA to complete, then clean up WaitForSingleObject(hThread, INFINITE); VirtualFreeEx(hProc, remoteMem, 0, MEM_RELEASE); CloseHandle(hThread); CloseHandle(hProc); return true; }

When LoadLibraryA runs in the target, Windows performs all standard DLL loading: maps the PE, resolves its imports from the target's loaded modules, applies base relocations if needed, and calls DllMain(hModule, DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, NULL). From that point, the DLL is a permanent resident of the target's memory and appears in the target's module list (queryable via EnumProcessModules).

Manual Mapping — Injecting Without LoadLibrary

Manual mapping bypasses the Windows loader entirely. Instead of asking the OS to load the DLL, the injector replicates what the loader does manually — reading the PE file, mapping its sections into the target, resolving imports, and applying relocations — all from outside the target process. The DLL never appears in the target's module list because LdrLoadDll was never called.

The manual mapping process involves these stages:

  1. Read the PE file into a local buffer. Parse the DOS header → NT headers → Optional header to find SizeOfImage, ImageBase, and the section table.
  2. Allocate a region of SizeOfImage bytes in the target process at any address (pass nullptr to let the OS choose, or attempt the preferred ImageBase).
  3. Copy each PE section (.text, .rdata, .data, etc.) from the raw file buffer to its correct virtual address in the target using WriteProcessMemory, respecting each section's VirtualAddress and SizeOfRawData.
  4. Apply relocations (the base relocation directory — IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_BASERELOC) if the image was not loaded at its preferred base. Each relocation entry patches an absolute address in the image.
  5. Resolve imports (the import directory — IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT). For each imported DLL, find it in the target's loaded modules, resolve each function's address, and write it into the target's Import Address Table (IAT).
  6. Set memory protections — mark .text as PAGE_EXECUTE_READ, .rdata as PAGE_READONLY, etc., using VirtualProtectEx.
  7. Call DllMain via a small shellcode or remote thread, passing the correct hModule, DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, and NULL arguments.
Note:Manual mapping reveals exactly what the Windows PE loader does internally — the same process occurs for every EXE and DLL Windows loads normally. Understanding manual mapping is equivalent to understanding the Windows loader architecture.

SetWindowsHookEx Injection — Riding the Message Loop

Windows has provided SetWindowsHookEx since Win16 as a legitimate API for intercepting system-wide events — keyboard input, mouse events, window messages. When you install a global hook that processes messages from a DLL (rather than an in-process callback), Windows automatically loads that DLL into every process that receives the hooked message type.

// hook_injector.cpp — conceptual overview // The DLL to inject must export the hook procedure. // In the injector process: HMODULE hHookDll = LoadLibraryA("hook_payload.dll"); HOOKPROC hookProc = (HOOKPROC)GetProcAddress(hHookDll, "GetMsgProc"); // WH_GETMESSAGE fires whenever a thread calls GetMessage() or PeekMessage() // Setting threadId=0 makes it GLOBAL — hits every GUI thread on the desktop HHOOK hHook = SetWindowsHookEx(WH_GETMESSAGE, hookProc, hHookDll, 0); // The first time any GUI thread in any process calls GetMessage(), // Windows loads hook_payload.dll into that process and calls GetMsgProc. // After the hook fires once, the DLL is resident. Call UnhookWindowsHookEx // to remove the hook (but the DLL stays loaded until the process exits). // ── Inside hook_payload.dll ────────────────────────────────────────────── LRESULT CALLBACK GetMsgProc(int nCode, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { static bool initialized = false; if (!initialized) { initialized = true; // This code runs in the target process context on first message CreateThread(nullptr, 0, WorkerThread, nullptr, 0, nullptr); } return CallNextHookEx(nullptr, nCode, wParam, lParam); }

This technique does not require OpenProcess or any direct process manipulation — it uses a documented, legitimate Windows API. The injected code runs on the target's own GUI thread (in the hook callback), then typically spawns a worker thread to avoid blocking message processing. Antivirus software flags global hooks from unknown publishers because they are a standard persistence and injection vector.

Accessibility software (screen readers, input method editors) relies on exactly this mechanism. WH_KEYBOARD hooks let input method editors intercept keystrokes before applications see them. WH_CBT hooks fire on window creation/destruction events and are used by UI automation frameworks.

Detection Methods Used by Security Software

Security software (anti-cheat engines, EDRs, AV products) uses a layered set of detection strategies. Understanding these is fundamental to building effective defenses:

  • API Monitoring (Kernel Callbacks): Windows provides kernel callbacks — PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine — that fire whenever a process is created or a module is loaded. Anti-cheat drivers register these to inspect every DLL load in protected processes. LoadLibrary-based injection is trivially detectable this way.
  • Module List Comparison: The target process's loaded module list (the PEB's Ldr.InMemoryOrderModuleList) can be walked and compared against an expected whitelist. Unknown modules trigger an alert. Manual mapping evades this because it never registers with the loader.
  • Memory Scanning: Scanning all executable memory regions for PE headers (MZ magic, PE\0\0 signature) that do not correspond to any registered module. Manual-mapped DLLs are found this way if they preserve their PE header in the allocation.
  • Thread Start Address Inspection: Enumerating all threads in a process and checking each thread's start address (via NtQueryInformationThread with ThreadQuerySetWin32StartAddress). Threads created by CreateRemoteThread pointing at LoadLibraryA or an unknown allocation are highly suspicious.
  • Integrity Checks: Hashing the bytes of loaded modules against known-good values. If a DLL's code section has been modified in memory (e.g., hooks installed), the hash mismatch is detectable.
  • Return Address Validation: Inline checks that verify the call stack does not include frames from unexpected modules — if a hook has been placed on a game function, the return address will point into the injected DLL rather than the game binary.
// Simplified detection: scan for orphaned PE headers in executable memory void ScanForUnregisteredModules(HANDLE hProcess) { MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION mbi{}; uintptr_t address = 0; const uint8_t MZ_MAGIC[] = { 0x4D, 0x5A }; // "MZ" while (VirtualQueryEx(hProcess, (LPCVOID)address, &mbi, sizeof(mbi)) == sizeof(mbi)) { if (mbi.State == MEM_COMMIT && mbi.Type == MEM_PRIVATE && // not MEM_IMAGE = not in module list (mbi.Protect & PAGE_EXECUTE_READ)) { uint8_t header[2]{}; SIZE_T bytesRead = 0; ReadProcessMemory(hProcess, mbi.BaseAddress, header, 2, &bytesRead); if (bytesRead == 2 && memcmp(header, MZ_MAGIC, 2) == 0) { // Found a PE header in private executable memory — suspicious printf("[!] Possible injected module at %p\n", mbi.BaseAddress); } } address = (uintptr_t)mbi.BaseAddress + mbi.RegionSize; } }

Legitimate Use Cases — Overlays, Modding, and Accessibility

DLL injection is not an inherently adversarial technique. Some of the most widely used software on Windows relies on it as a core architectural component:

  • Steam Overlay (GameOverlayRenderer64.dll): Injected into every Steam game to render the in-game overlay, handle the Shift+Tab shortcut, manage friend notifications, and enable screenshot capture. Uses a combination of SetWindowsHookEx and Direct3D/Vulkan present hook to intercept the swap chain.
  • Discord Overlay (DiscordHook64.dll): Injected to render voice chat indicators and notifications on top of game frames. Hooks DirectX and OpenGL present calls in the target process. Explicitly whitelisted by most anti-cheat systems.
  • NVIDIA GeForce Experience / NvCamera: Injects to enable the in-game performance overlay (Alt+Z), screenshot, and video capture. The NvCamera DLL hooks the graphics API within the game process.
  • RenderDoc: A graphics debugger widely used by game developers. Injects a capture DLL to intercept all D3D11/D3D12/Vulkan API calls, record GPU commands, and enable frame replay.
  • Script Extenders (SKSE, F4SE, etc.): The Skyrim Script Extender injects into the game process to extend the scripting engine with new functions, enabling the complex mod ecosystem. Entirely community-built and fully legitimate.
  • Screen Readers (NVDA, JAWS): Inject accessibility hooks into browsers and applications to read UI element text that is not exposed through standard Win32 accessibility APIs.
Key Takeaway:The technique itself is neutral — it is a documented capability of the Windows process model. Context and intent determine legitimacy. Understanding injection mechanics enables building better detection systems, evaluating anti-cheat effectiveness, and building tools that operate correctly alongside the many legitimate injectors already present in a typical gaming setup.

1. IDA Pro vs. Ghidra — Choosing Your Tool

Both IDA Pro and Ghidra are production-grade disassemblers and decompilers capable of analyzing stripped 64-bit PE binaries (the format used by most Windows games). The choice between them comes down to cost, ecosystem, and personal workflow.

IDA Pro (Hex-Rays) is the long-standing industry standard. Its disassembler is widely regarded as the most accurate available, and the Hex-Rays Decompiler plugin produces cleaner C pseudo-code than most alternatives. IDA's type reconstruction, structure layout editor, and scripting API (IDAPython) are mature and well-documented. The tradeoff is cost — a perpetual license for IDA Pro with the Hex-Rays x64 decompiler exceeds $3,000 USD. There is a free tier called IDA Free (limited to 32-bit x86 analysis) and cloud decompilation via Dogbolt / hex-rays.com for quick one-off analysis.

Ghidra was developed by the NSA's Research Directorate and released as open source in 2019. It is completely free, supports a wide range of processor architectures (x86-16/32/64, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, and dozens more), and includes a built-in decompiler that produces C pseudo-code of comparable quality to Hex-Rays for most game analysis tasks. Its scripting API (Ghidra Script, Java or Python via Jython) and plugin ecosystem have grown substantially since release. For the purposes of game security research, Ghidra is an excellent and sufficient choice.

  • Cost: IDA Pro — paid ($3k+) | Ghidra — free
  • Decompiler quality: IDA Hex-Rays — excellent | Ghidra — very good, occasional artifacts
  • Scripting: IDA — IDAPython (mature) | Ghidra — Java / Jython / GhidraScript
  • Plugin ecosystem: IDA — large, commercial plugins available | Ghidra — growing, all open source
  • PDB support: Both support importing Microsoft PDB files for symbol-assisted analysis

2. Loading a Game Binary in Ghidra

Ghidra requires Java 17 or later. Download from ghidra-sre.org, extract the archive, and run ghidraRun.bat (Windows) or ghidraRun (Linux/macOS). No installation is required — Ghidra is fully portable.

  1. Create a project: File → New Project → Non-Shared Project. Give it a name matching the game. Projects store all your analysis, annotations, and renamed symbols — treat them as the primary output of your research.
  2. Import the binary: File → Import File → select the game's main .exe. Ghidra will auto-detect the format. For most modern Windows games you will see:
    Format: Portable Executable (PE) Language: x86:LE:64:default:windows ← 64-bit x86, little-endian Compiler: windows ← MSVC detection
  3. Load PDB if available: If the game ships with a PDB file (some older or indie games do), Ghidra will offer to apply it. This populates function names, type information, and global variable names, saving enormous amounts of manual work. Accept this — it is one of the highest-leverage actions available.
  4. Run auto-analysis: After import, Ghidra prompts to analyze. Accept the defaults. The analysis phase disassembles the entire binary, identifies function boundaries, recovers call graphs, and applies FLIRT-style signature matching to identify standard library functions (CRT, STL, etc.). This takes 1–20 minutes depending on binary size.
Note:Never analyze the actual game binary that the game runs from. Copy the .exe and any associated .dll files you want to analyze to your research directory first. Ghidra may lock the file, and you want the original untouched for comparison across patches.

3. The Decompiler View — Reading C Pseudo-code

Click any function in the Symbol Tree or double-click an address in the Listing (disassembly) view. The Decompiler window on the right shows Ghidra's C pseudo-code reconstruction. This is not the original source code — it is a best-effort reconstruction from machine instructions, and it contains artifacts.

Here is a simplified example of what Ghidra's decompiler output typically looks like for a stripped player update function before any annotation:

// Ghidra decompiler output — BEFORE annotation // Function: FUN_140123ab0 (auto-generated name) void FUN_140123ab0(longlong param_1, float param_2) { float fVar1; float fVar2; longlong *plVar3; if (*(int *)(param_1 + 0x18) != 0) { // health check fVar1 = *(float *)(param_1 + 0x44); // current X velocity fVar2 = *(float *)(param_1 + 0x48); // current Y velocity fVar1 = fVar1 + *(float *)(param_1 + 0x8c) * param_2; // integrate X fVar2 = fVar2 + *(float *)(param_1 + 0x94) * param_2; // integrate Y *(float *)(param_1 + 0x44) = fVar1; *(float *)(param_1 + 0x48) = fVar2; *(float *)(param_1 + 0x3c) = *(float *)(param_1 + 0x3c) + fVar1 * param_2; *(float *)(param_1 + 0x40) = *(float *)(param_1 + 0x40) + fVar2 * param_2; plVar3 = *(longlong **)(param_1 + 0x100); // pointer to another object if (plVar3 != (longlong *)0x0) { FUN_14009af20(plVar3, param_1); // call on child object } } return; }

Common decompiler artifacts to be aware of:

  • Raw offset access like *(float *)(param_1 + 0x44) — this means the compiler optimized away a named struct member. The offset 0x44 is the byte offset into a class/struct. Collecting these offsets is how you reconstruct class layouts.
  • Auto-generated names like FUN_140123ab0, param_1, fVar1 — rename these as you understand them. Use Ghidra's L key shortcut to rename any symbol.
  • Inlined functions — Small functions get inlined by the compiler and appear as inline code in the caller's decompilation. They won't have separate function entries in the Symbol Tree.
  • Type confusion — Ghidra may represent a float field as an int or vice versa if it can't determine the type from context alone. Right-click a variable and use Retype Variable to correct this.

4. Finding Interesting Functions

A stripped game binary contains thousands of unnamed functions. The challenge is navigating to the ones relevant to your research. The following techniques are the most effective entry points:

String reference search: Games frequently log errors or debug messages as string literals embedded in the binary. These strings survive stripping. Search → For Strings, filter by a known term (e.g., "PlayerController", "health", "damage", "spawn"), then use cross-references (right-click → References → Find References) to navigate to the code that uses each string. The surrounding code is often exactly the function you want.

# Ghidra Script example: Find all functions that reference a specific string # Run via: Window → Script Manager → New Script → Python from ghidra.program.model.symbol import SymbolType target_string = "PlayerTakeDamage" # Find the string in the defined data data_iter = currentProgram.getListing().getDefinedData(True) for data in data_iter: if data.hasStringValue() and target_string in str(data.getValue()): addr = data.getAddress() print(f"Found string at: {addr}") # Get all code references to this string address refs = getReferencesTo(addr) for ref in refs: fn = getFunctionContaining(ref.getFromAddress()) if fn: print(f" Referenced in function: {fn.getName()} @ {fn.getEntryPoint()}")

Import table analysis: Look at the binary's imports (Window → Symbol Tree → Imports). Calls to VirtualAlloc, custom memory allocators, or STL container functions give clues about memory management patterns. Functions importing GetAsyncKeyState or XInputGetState lead to input handling.

Function size heuristics: Sort the function list by size (Window → Symbol Tree → Functions, right-click header → Column Settings → add Size). Very large functions (2000+ instructions) are often update loops, game state managers, or physics solvers — prime targets for reverse engineering.

5. Identifying Entity and Player Structures

In C++ games, player and entity data is stored in class instances (objects). The decompiler represents field accesses as *(type *)(param + offset) patterns. When you see the same parameter accessed repeatedly at different offsets across many functions, that parameter is almost certainly a pointer to a key class instance (e.g., CPlayer, EntityBase, ACharacter).

The workflow for reconstructing a structure:

  1. Find a function that clearly operates on a player object (e.g., a damage function found via string search for "damage" or "health").
  2. Note every offset accessed on the first parameter. Each unique offset is a struct field. Common patterns: floats at small offsets (4, 8, 12) are often position/velocity; small integers at mid-range offsets (0x10–0x30) are IDs or flags; floats in the 0x3C–0x50 range in update functions are often health/mana values.
  3. Use Ghidra's Data Type Manager (Window → Data Type Manager) to create a new Structure type. Add fields at each discovered offset with their inferred types.
  4. Retype param_1 in the function to your new structure pointer type (right-click → Retype Variable → select your struct). Ghidra will immediately update all field accesses in the decompiler to use named members.
// Before retyping param_1: if (*(int *)(param_1 + 0x18) != 0) { fVar1 = *(float *)(param_1 + 0x3c); // After creating struct CPlayer and retyping: if (player->isAlive != 0) { fVar1 = player->health;

Cross-reference the structure pointer globally — right-click the parameter → References → Find References to Symbol. Ghidra will show every function that receives the same pointer type, giving you a list of all methods that operate on the class. This is the game-RE equivalent of recovering a class's method table.

6. Renaming, Annotating, and Exporting Findings

Reverse engineering is a long iterative process. The value of a Ghidra project compounds over time as you accumulate annotations. Consistent renaming practices are essential.

  • Rename functions (L key): Use a consistent naming convention. A common scheme is ClassName__MethodName (e.g., CPlayer__TakeDamage, CPlayer__Update). This makes the Symbol Tree navigable and searchable.
  • Add comments (semicolon key): Add end-of-line comments explaining non-obvious behavior. Pre-plate (function header) comments via right-click → Set Function Comment explain what the function does at a high level.
  • Bookmarks: Use Window → Bookmarks to mark important addresses. Categories like "PlayerCode", "Rendering", "NetworkManager" help navigate a large project.
  • Exporting offsets to code: Once you have identified key offsets, export them to a C++ header file for use in your research tool:
// offsets.h — Generated from Ghidra analysis of game v1.42.0 // Binary hash (SHA256): a1b2c3d4... #pragma once #include <cstdint> // CPlayer offsets (relative to CPlayer* this pointer) namespace Offsets { namespace CPlayer { constexpr uintptr_t isAlive = 0x18; // int32 constexpr uintptr_t health = 0x3C; // float constexpr uintptr_t maxHealth = 0x40; // float constexpr uintptr_t positionX = 0x44; // float constexpr uintptr_t positionY = 0x48; // float constexpr uintptr_t positionZ = 0x4C; // float constexpr uintptr_t velocityX = 0x8C; // float constexpr uintptr_t velocityY = 0x94; // float constexpr uintptr_t teamId = 0xB0; // int32 constexpr uintptr_t pWeaponSlot = 0x100; // CWeapon* } // Static offsets from module base (game.exe) namespace Static { constexpr uintptr_t pLocalPlayer = 0x01A2B3C0; // CPlayer** constexpr uintptr_t pEntityList = 0x01A2C000; // CEntityList* } }

Save your Ghidra project regularly (File → Save Project). Projects can be exported as Ghidra Archive files (.gar) and shared with collaborators — the entire annotated analysis travels with the archive, minus the original binary.

Note:Offsets change with every game patch. Version your offsets.h file and tag it with the game version and binary hash so you know exactly which build the offsets are valid for. A single incorrect offset will produce silent data corruption in your research tool.

1. Why Software Implements Anti-Debugging

Anti-debugging serves several legitimate purposes in commercial software. Understanding the motivation behind a technique helps you assess how robust its implementation is likely to be.

  • Game integrity protection: Online game anti-cheat systems (BattlEye, EAC, Vanguard, VAC) use anti-debugging to prevent cheating tools from attaching to game processes and reading or modifying game state in real time. If a debugger is detected, the game either kicks the player or terminates.
  • License enforcement: Commercial software uses anti-debugging to slow down reverse engineers attempting to bypass licensing checks. If a debugger is detected near a license validation routine, the software may silently pass a fake "licensed" check to waste the researcher's time.
  • Malware self-protection: Malicious software uses anti-debugging to resist dynamic analysis in sandboxes and by malware researchers. This is the adversarial use case — understanding these techniques is how security researchers build better sandboxes and analysis pipelines.
  • Copy protection / DRM: Systems like Denuvo use layers of anti-debugging to protect their virtualized license-check code from being traced or extracted.

2. IsDebuggerPresent and the PEB Flag

IsDebuggerPresent() is the simplest and most widely used anti-debugging check. It is a single-instruction read from the Process Environment Block (PEB) — the per-process data structure maintained by the Windows kernel that stores process metadata.

The PEB is located at gs:[0x60] on x86-64 Windows. Offset 0x02 into the PEB is the BeingDebugged byte — Windows sets this to 1 when a debugger attaches via the standard debug API, and 0 otherwise. IsDebuggerPresent simply reads this byte:

// Implementation side — how a game checks for a debugger #include <Windows.h> bool IsBeingDebugged_API() { // Standard Win32 API — reads PEB.BeingDebugged return IsDebuggerPresent() != FALSE; } bool IsBeingDebugged_Manual() { // Direct PEB read without calling the API // (harder to hook since there's no function call to intercept) BOOL result = FALSE; #ifdef _WIN64 __asm { // x86-64: GS segment register points to TEB // TEB + 0x60 = PEB pointer // PEB + 0x02 = BeingDebugged byte } // Intrinsic equivalent: result = *(BOOL *)(__readgsqword(0x60) + 0x02); #else // x86-32: FS:[0x30] = PEB result = *(BOOL *)(__readfsdword(0x30) + 0x02); #endif return result != FALSE; } // PEB.NtGlobalFlag — a secondary indicator // When a process is created under a debugger, NtGlobalFlag // is set to 0x70 (FLG_HEAP_ENABLE_TAIL_CHECK | // FLG_HEAP_ENABLE_FREE_CHECK | // FLG_HEAP_VALIDATE_PARAMETERS) // Normal processes have NtGlobalFlag = 0x00 bool CheckNtGlobalFlag() { #ifdef _WIN64 DWORD ntGlobalFlag = *(DWORD *)(__readgsqword(0x60) + 0xBC); #else DWORD ntGlobalFlag = *(DWORD *)(__readfsdword(0x30) + 0x68); #endif return (ntGlobalFlag & 0x70) != 0; } // ------------------------------------------------------- // Research / analysis side — patching these checks // ------------------------------------------------------- // Method 1: Patch PEB.BeingDebugged to 0 at runtime // In x64dbg: Go to PEB address (view PEB in memory map), // navigate to offset 0x02, change byte from 0x01 to 0x00. // // Method 2: Patch the call site in the binary // In x64dbg, find the IsDebuggerPresent call: // Example disassembly: // call qword ptr [<&IsDebuggerPresent>] // test eax, eax // jne detected_label ; <- patch this to jmp (unconditional) // // Method 3: Use ScyllaHide plugin for x64dbg // ScyllaHide intercepts all standard debug-detection APIs at // the NTDLL level and returns "not being debugged" regardless. // Options > ScyllaHide > select a preset matching your target.

3. NtQueryInformationProcess — Kernel-Level Detection

NtQueryInformationProcess is an undocumented NTAPI function (exported from ntdll.dll) that queries a wide range of per-process information from the kernel. Two information classes are commonly used for debugger detection:

  • ProcessDebugPort (class 7): Returns a nonzero port handle if a user-mode debugger is attached. This check is more reliable than IsDebuggerPresent because it queries kernel state rather than the user-mode PEB, which can be trivially patched.
  • ProcessDebugObjectHandle (class 30): Returns a handle to the debug object created by the debugger. If this call succeeds with a non-NULL handle, a debugger is present. On Windows Vista+, closing this handle with CloseHandle raises an exception when a debugger is present.
#include <Windows.h> #include <winternl.h> // NtQueryInformationProcess is not in standard headers for these classes. // We resolve it dynamically from ntdll.dll. typedef NTSTATUS (WINAPI *pNtQueryInformationProcess)( HANDLE, PROCESSINFOCLASS, PVOID, ULONG, PULONG ); // Information class values not in public headers: #define ProcessDebugPort ((PROCESSINFOCLASS)7) #define ProcessDebugObjectHandle ((PROCESSINFOCLASS)30) #define ProcessDebugFlags ((PROCESSINFOCLASS)31) bool CheckDebugPort() { auto NtQIP = (pNtQueryInformationProcess)GetProcAddress( GetModuleHandleA("ntdll.dll"), "NtQueryInformationProcess" ); if (!NtQIP) return false; DWORD_PTR debugPort = 0; NTSTATUS status = NtQIP( GetCurrentProcess(), ProcessDebugPort, &debugPort, sizeof(debugPort), nullptr ); // If status == STATUS_SUCCESS and debugPort != 0, debugger is present return NT_SUCCESS(status) && (debugPort != 0); } bool CheckDebugObjectHandle() { auto NtQIP = (pNtQueryInformationProcess)GetProcAddress( GetModuleHandleA("ntdll.dll"), "NtQueryInformationProcess" ); if (!NtQIP) return false; HANDLE hDebugObject = nullptr; NTSTATUS status = NtQIP( GetCurrentProcess(), ProcessDebugObjectHandle, &hDebugObject, sizeof(hDebugObject), nullptr ); if (NT_SUCCESS(status) && hDebugObject != nullptr) { CloseHandle(hDebugObject); return true; // debugger present } return false; } // ------------------------------------------------------- // Research / analysis side // ------------------------------------------------------- // NtQueryInformationProcess checks require hooking at the // syscall level or patching the return value. // // ScyllaHide handles ProcessDebugPort and ProcessDebugObjectHandle // automatically in its "NtQueryInformationProcess" hook settings. // // Manual approach with x64dbg: // Set a breakpoint on ntdll!NtQueryInformationProcess. // When it triggers with ProcessDebugPort as class: // - Let the call complete (F9 to return) // - Find the output variable on the stack and zero it out // - Resume — the check sees 0 (no debugger)

4. Timing Checks — RDTSC and GetTickCount

When a process is being single-stepped through a debugger, or when a breakpoint causes an exception that the debugger handles, execution pauses for a human-scale interval — milliseconds to seconds — before continuing. Timing-based anti-debug techniques exploit this: measure elapsed time between two points, and if the elapsed time is far greater than the expected execution time, a debugger must be present.

RDTSC (Read Time-Stamp Counter) is an x86 instruction that reads the CPU's cycle counter — a 64-bit value that increments every CPU clock cycle. It has nanosecond-level resolution and is much harder to fake than API-based time functions.

#include <Windows.h> #include <intrin.h> // for __rdtsc() // --- RDTSC timing check --- bool TimingCheck_RDTSC() { UINT64 t1 = __rdtsc(); // Execute a known-cost operation (or just a few NOPs) volatile int dummy = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) dummy += i; UINT64 t2 = __rdtsc(); UINT64 elapsed = t2 - t1; // Under normal execution: ~few hundred cycles. // Under a debugger with a breakpoint nearby: millions+ cycles. // Threshold must be tuned per CPU and operation complexity. return elapsed > 1'000'000ULL; // >1M cycles = suspiciously slow } // --- GetTickCount / QueryPerformanceCounter check --- bool TimingCheck_QPC() { LARGE_INTEGER freq, t1, t2; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&freq); QueryPerformanceCounter(&t1); // Placeholder for the code block being timed volatile int x = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) x ^= i; QueryPerformanceCounter(&t2); // Calculate elapsed time in microseconds LONGLONG elapsedUs = (t2.QuadPart - t1.QuadPart) * 1'000'000LL / freq.QuadPart; // Flag if > 5 milliseconds for this trivial loop return elapsedUs > 5000LL; } // ------------------------------------------------------- // Research / analysis side // ------------------------------------------------------- // Timing checks are defeated by running the target WITHOUT // stopping at breakpoints inside the timed region. // // Approach 1: Run to just before the timing check, let it // execute uninterrupted (no breakpoints inside), then // set a breakpoint after the comparison. // // Approach 2: Patch the comparison instruction. // Find the JA/JG/JNZ after the elapsed time comparison // in the disassembly and NOP it or invert it to JNA/JLE/JZ. // // Approach 3: Hook __rdtsc via CPUID trap (advanced). // On some hypervisors you can intercept RDTSC exits and // return controlled values — this is how some sandboxes // handle timing-based evasion.

5. The OutputDebugString Trick

OutputDebugString sends a string to a debugger attached to the process. The behavioral difference between the debugger-present and no-debugger cases creates a detectable side effect that older protection systems exploited as a lightweight check. This technique is largely historical on modern Windows but still appears in legacy games and protections.

The trick works through Windows' error code behavior:

  • When no debugger is present, OutputDebugString raises exception 0x40010006 internally. Because no debugger is listening, the OS handles it and returns normally. GetLastError() after the call returns ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE (6).
  • When a debugger is present, the debugger intercepts the exception, processes the string, and resumes. GetLastError() after the call returns 0 (no error), because the error code was cleared by the exception handling path.
#include <Windows.h> // Implementation side — OutputDebugString-based check // Note: Behavior is Windows-version dependent. On Windows 10+ // this technique is unreliable without additional conditions. bool IsDebuggerPresent_OutputDebugString() { // Deliberately set a known last error SetLastError(0xDEADBEEF); // Call OutputDebugString OutputDebugStringA("test"); // If a debugger consumed the string, last error was reset to 0. // If no debugger, last error remains 0xDEADBEEF or becomes // ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE. DWORD err = GetLastError(); return (err == 0); } // ------------------------------------------------------- // Research / analysis side // ------------------------------------------------------- // Method 1: Hook OutputDebugStringA/W in the import table // Replace the IAT entry for OutputDebugStringA with a stub // that sets GetLastError to a non-zero value and returns. // // Method 2: Use a debugger plugin that silences these exceptions. // In x64dbg: Options → Preferences → Exceptions // Add exception code 0x40010006 to the "ignore" list. // The debugger will silently continue past it, leaving // the last error unchanged. // // Method 3: NOP the conditional jump after GetLastError() // in the check function.

6. TLS Callbacks — Code Before the Entry Point

Thread Local Storage (TLS) callbacks are a feature of the PE file format that allows code to execute automatically when a thread starts or stops — and critically, before WinMain or DllMain is called. This makes them an effective location for early anti-debugging checks, because many researchers set their first breakpoint at WinMain or the PE entry point, unwittingly letting the TLS callback detection code run unobserved first.

A PE can have multiple TLS callbacks registered in its .tls section via the IMAGE_TLS_DIRECTORY structure. The OS loader calls each callback in order before handing control to the entry point.

// Implementation side — registering a TLS callback in MSVC #include <Windows.h> // Forward declaration of our TLS callback function void NTAPI TlsCallback(PVOID DllHandle, DWORD Reason, PVOID Reserved); // Register the callback by placing a pointer to it in the // .CRT$XLB section. The linker merges all .CRT$XL? sections // and the loader calls each function pointer at thread init time. #pragma comment(linker, "/INCLUDE:__tls_used") #pragma data_seg(".CRT$XLB") PIMAGE_TLS_CALLBACK _tls_callback_ptr = TlsCallback; #pragma data_seg() void NTAPI TlsCallback(PVOID DllHandle, DWORD Reason, PVOID Reserved) { // DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH fires once on process start — before WinMain. if (Reason == DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) { // Perform any anti-debug check here. // This code runs BEFORE the first WinMain breakpoint. if (IsDebuggerPresent()) { // Options: terminate silently, corrupt state, // or set a flag for later detection. // For research purposes, we just note the detection. OutputDebugStringA("[TLS] Debugger detected in TLS callback. "); ExitProcess(0); } // Check PEB.NtGlobalFlag (set by debug heap when under debugger) #ifdef _WIN64 DWORD ntGlobalFlag = *(DWORD *)(__readgsqword(0x60) + 0xBC); #else DWORD ntGlobalFlag = *(DWORD *)(__readfsdword(0x30) + 0x68); #endif if (ntGlobalFlag & 0x70) { ExitProcess(0); } } } int main() { // By the time we reach here, TlsCallback has already executed. // The TLS callback ran before this line. return 0; } // ------------------------------------------------------- // Research / analysis side // ------------------------------------------------------- // Finding TLS callbacks: // - In x64dbg: Options > Preferences > Events // Enable "TLS Callbacks" — the debugger will break // at the start of each TLS callback before they execute. // // - In Ghidra: Open the PE's Headers in the listing. // Navigate to IMAGE_TLS_DIRECTORY → AddressOfCallBacks. // Each pointer in the array is a TLS callback. Double-click // to jump to the callback function and analyze it. // // - Patching: Once you locate the TLS callback function in // x64dbg, set a breakpoint at its entry. When it breaks, // simply NOP out the IsDebuggerPresent call and its // conditional jump, then continue normally.
Practical tip for researchers:When first analyzing an unknown binary, always enable TLS callback interception in your debugger before running. In x64dbg this is under Options → Preferences → Events → "Break on TLS Callbacks". Missing TLS callbacks is one of the most common reasons a protection appears to "magically" detect a debugger before any code you've analyzed runs.
Layered defenses:Modern game anti-cheat systems (Vanguard, EasyAntiCheat, BattlEye) combine multiple detection methods simultaneously — PEB checks, NtQueryInformationProcess, kernel callbacks, timing, driver presence detection, and more. Defeating one layer in isolation is rarely sufficient; a production-grade analysis requires addressing all layers, typically requiring kernel-level tooling (a custom driver or hypervisor-based debugger such as WinDbg with a kernel debugging connection or VirtualKD).

windows-kernel-drivers:
User Mode vs. Kernel Mode — Ring 3 vs. Ring 0

Modern x86-64 CPUs implement four privilege rings (0–3). Windows uses only two in practice:

  • Ring 3 (User Mode): Where all standard applications run — browsers, games, your own executables. Code here is sandboxed: each process gets its own virtual address space, and the CPU prevents direct hardware access. Attempts to execute privileged instructions (like IN, OUT, or LGDT) cause a General Protection Fault and the OS kills the process. Win32 API calls that need kernel services cross into Ring 0 via a syscall instruction, which traps into the kernel.
  • Ring 0 (Kernel Mode): Where the Windows Executive, HAL, and all kernel-mode drivers run. Code here can access any physical memory address, execute any instruction, and manipulate CPU control registers. A single bad pointer dereference at Ring 0 triggers a Blue Screen of Death (BSOD) — there is no safety net.

From a research perspective, Ring 0 access means you can read or write any process's memory without the target process being aware, hook system calls before they are processed, and interact with hardware directly. This is why anti-cheat software often runs kernel drivers — they operate at the same privilege level they are protecting against.

User Mode (Ring 3) Kernel Mode (Ring 0) ──────────────────── ────────────────────────────── Your game process ntoskrnl.exe (Windows Executive) Discord overlay DLL hal.dll (Hardware Abstraction) System DLLs (ntdll, kernel32) Driver1.sys, Driver2.sys ... ↕ syscall / DeviceIoControl ↕ Transition via software interrupt or SYSCALL instruction

Driver Types: WDM, KMDF, and UMDF

Microsoft has evolved its driver framework over the decades. Choosing the right model matters for both functionality and stability:

  • WDM (Windows Driver Model): The foundational layer — raw access to kernel APIs. You manage your own IRPs (I/O Request Packets), device objects, and dispatch routines manually. Maximum flexibility, maximum responsibility. Most legacy drivers and research/proof-of-concept drivers use WDM because it has the fewest abstractions. If something goes wrong, it is your fault entirely.
  • KMDF (Kernel-Mode Driver Framework): A structured framework built on top of WDM. KMDF abstracts the IRP lifecycle, power management, plug-and-play events, and synchronization primitives into callback-based objects (WDFDEVICE, WDFQUEUE, WDFREQUEST). It dramatically reduces boilerplate and common crash vectors. Use KMDF for any production driver where you do not specifically need WDM's raw control.
  • UMDF (User-Mode Driver Framework): Drivers that run in user space but appear as kernel drivers to the I/O manager. Suitable for protocol drivers, USB HID devices, and sensors where a crash should not BSOD the machine. Cannot read arbitrary process memory or interact with kernel structures — not applicable to security research scenarios.
Recommendation:For security research and game tooling, start with WDM to understand the raw primitives. Once comfortable, migrate to KMDF for any code you intend to ship — it handles dozens of edge cases (cancel-safe queues, reference counting, device removal) automatically.

Setting Up the Windows Driver Kit (WDK) with Visual Studio

Driver development requires a matched pair of Visual Studio and the Windows Driver Kit (WDK). Both versions must align exactly — a WDK for Windows 11 24H2 will not work against a Windows 10 SDK.

  1. Install Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload. Ensure the Windows SDK component is checked (version 10.0.22621 or later for modern targets).
  2. Download the WDK from learn.microsoft.com/windows-hardware/drivers/download-the-wdk. Run the installer — it will offer to install the VS extension automatically.
  3. In Visual Studio, create a new project → search for "Kernel Mode Driver, Empty (KMDF)" or "Kernel Mode Driver, Empty (WDM)". The templates set up the correct compiler flags (/kernel, floating-point restrictions) and linker settings (/DRIVER:WDM, entry point DriverEntry).
  4. Set up a test VM (Hyper-V or VMware) running Windows. Enable kernel debugging over a network or COM port. Never test experimental drivers on your development host — a BSOD loop can corrupt the filesystem.
# In the test VM — enable kernel debugging over network (kdnet): bcdedit /debug on bcdedit /dbgsettings net hostip:<DEV_MACHINE_IP> port:50000 key:1.2.3.4 # On the dev machine — attach WinDbg Preview: # File → Kernel Debug → Net → fill in port and key

A Minimal Driver Skeleton — DriverEntry and Unload

Every kernel driver must export a DriverEntry function — the kernel calls this once when the driver is loaded, analogous to main() in a user-mode application. Below is the smallest correct WDM driver that creates a device, registers a symbolic link (so user-mode can open it), and cleans up on unload.

// minimal_driver.c #include <ntddk.h> #define DEVICE_NAME L"\Device\MinimalDriver" #define SYMLINK_NAME L"\DosDevices\MinimalDriver" PDEVICE_OBJECT g_DeviceObject = NULL; // Called when the driver is unloaded (e.g., sc stop MinimalDriver) VOID DriverUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT DriverObject) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(DriverObject); // Remove the symbolic link so user-mode can no longer open it UNICODE_STRING symlinkName; RtlInitUnicodeString(&symlinkName, SYMLINK_NAME); IoDeleteSymbolicLink(&symlinkName); // Delete the device object if (g_DeviceObject) IoDeleteDevice(g_DeviceObject); DbgPrint("[MinimalDriver] Unloaded.
"); } // Handles IRP_MJ_CREATE and IRP_MJ_CLOSE — just complete them successfully NTSTATUS DispatchCreateClose(PDEVICE_OBJECT DeviceObject, PIRP Irp) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(DeviceObject); Irp->IoStatus.Status = STATUS_SUCCESS; Irp->IoStatus.Information = 0; IoCompleteRequest(Irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } // Kernel entry point — runs at IRQL PASSIVE_LEVEL NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT DriverObject, PUNICODE_STRING RegistryPath) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(RegistryPath); DbgPrint("[MinimalDriver] Loading...
"); // Register the unload routine (without this, the driver cannot be stopped) DriverObject->DriverUnload = DriverUnload; // Register dispatch routines for open/close DriverObject->MajorFunction[IRP_MJ_CREATE] = DispatchCreateClose; DriverObject->MajorFunction[IRP_MJ_CLOSE] = DispatchCreateClose; // Create the device object UNICODE_STRING deviceName; RtlInitUnicodeString(&deviceName, DEVICE_NAME); NTSTATUS status = IoCreateDevice( DriverObject, 0, // DeviceExtension size (0 = none) &deviceName, FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, FALSE, // not exclusive &g_DeviceObject ); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) { DbgPrint("[MinimalDriver] IoCreateDevice failed: 0x%X
", status); return status; } // Create symbolic link accessible from user mode as \.\MinimalDriver UNICODE_STRING symlinkName; RtlInitUnicodeString(&symlinkName, SYMLINK_NAME); status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&symlinkName, &deviceName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) { IoDeleteDevice(g_DeviceObject); return status; } DbgPrint("[MinimalDriver] Loaded successfully.
"); return STATUS_SUCCESS; }

The DRIVER_OBJECT structure passed into DriverEntry is the kernel's representation of your driver. Populating its MajorFunction dispatch table — an array of 28 function pointers indexed by IRP major code — is how you register handlers for all I/O operations (create, read, write, IOCTL, cleanup, close, etc.).

IOCTL Communication — User Mode to Kernel Mode

The standard mechanism for a user-mode application to send commands to a kernel driver is IOCTL (I/O Control Code). The user side calls DeviceIoControl(); the kernel dispatch routine for IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL receives the call with a structured IRP.

// Shared header (used by both driver and user-mode app) // shared.h #pragma once #include <Windows.h> // user side; use <ntddk.h> equivalent in driver // CTL_CODE macro: DeviceType | Function | Method | Access #define IOCTL_READ_MEMORY CTL_CODE(FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, 0x800, \ METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS) typedef struct _READ_REQUEST { ULONG_PTR TargetPid; ULONG_PTR Address; SIZE_T Size; } READ_REQUEST, *PREAD_REQUEST; // ── Kernel-side IOCTL handler ───────────────────────────────────────────── NTSTATUS DispatchIoControl(PDEVICE_OBJECT DeviceObject, PIRP Irp) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(DeviceObject); PIO_STACK_LOCATION stack = IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(Irp); ULONG code = stack->Parameters.DeviceIoControl.IoControlCode; ULONG inLen = stack->Parameters.DeviceIoControl.InputBufferLength; NTSTATUS status = STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST; ULONG_PTR info = 0; if (code == IOCTL_READ_MEMORY && inLen >= sizeof(READ_REQUEST)) { PREAD_REQUEST req = (PREAD_REQUEST)Irp->AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer; // ... locate target process, call MmCopyVirtualMemory, etc. status = STATUS_SUCCESS; info = req->Size; } Irp->IoStatus.Status = status; Irp->IoStatus.Information = info; IoCompleteRequest(Irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return status; } // ── User-mode app side ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── // user_app.c (compiled as regular Win32 executable) HANDLE hDriver = CreateFile(L"\\.\MinimalDriver", GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE, 0, NULL, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, NULL); READ_REQUEST req = { .TargetPid = targetPid, .Address = 0x7FF600000000ULL, .Size = 4 }; DWORD bytesReturned = 0; DeviceIoControl(hDriver, IOCTL_READ_MEMORY, &req, sizeof(req), outputBuf, sizeof(outputBuf), &bytesReturned, NULL);

The METHOD_BUFFERED transfer type (the third field of CTL_CODE) tells the I/O manager to copy both the input and output buffers into a single kernel-allocated buffer (Irp->AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer), which you access safely from your dispatch routine. Other methods (METHOD_IN_DIRECT, METHOD_NEITHER) give different tradeoffs between safety and performance.

Test Signing vs. Production Signing

Since Windows Vista 64-bit, the kernel enforces Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE): every .sys file loaded by the kernel must be signed by a trusted certificate authority. Unsigned drivers are blocked before DriverEntry is ever called.

  • Test Mode: Allows drivers signed with any self-signed certificate (created via makecert or the WDK's signtool). Enable it in the test VM with:
    bcdedit /set testsigning on # Reboot required. A watermark appears in the bottom-right of the desktop.
  • EV Code Signing Certificate: For drivers you distribute to end users, you need an Extended Validation (EV) code signing certificate from a Microsoft-approved CA (DigiCert, Sectigo, etc.). These cost ~$400–700/year and require identity verification.
  • WHQL (Windows Hardware Quality Labs): The gold standard — Microsoft tests your driver and adds it to the trusted list. Required for drivers that must install without any security prompts across all Windows configurations. Obtained through the Windows Hardware Dev Center portal.
# Create a self-signed test certificate (development only) makecert -r -pe -ss PrivateCertStore -n "CN=TestDriverCert" TestCert.cer certmgr /add TestCert.cer /s /r localMachine root certmgr /add TestCert.cer /s /r localMachine trustedpublisher # Sign the .sys file signtool sign /v /s PrivateCertStore /n "TestDriverCert" \ /t http://timestamp.digicert.com MinimalDriver.sys # Verify signature signtool verify /v /pa MinimalDriver.sys
